entry.title: Covariate-adaptive randomization using historical data and bootstrap-based inference

link.title: Covariate-adaptive randomization using historical data and bootstrap-based inference

entry.content:
Covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR) can improve the efficiency of average treatment effect (ATE) estimation by reducing chance imbalances in prognostic baseline covariates. A recently proposed CAR method that balances multiple covariates, including continuous ones, can achieve optimal precision when the conditional mean of the outcome can be expressed as a linear combination of the covariate features used for the CAR procedure. However, this condition may be difficult to satisfy when the relationship between covariates and the outcome is nonlinear. Furthermore, directly balancing multiple covariates may reduce estimation precision in finite samples. We propose three CAR methods that incorporate a prognostic score learned from individual-level historical data into their imbalance measures. The prognostic score reduces multiple covariates to one dimension while giving larger weights to covariates that are more strongly associated with the outcome. Another challenge with CAR is difficulty in inference due to dependence between subjects induced by the CAR procedure. Existing bootstrap-based inference methods emulate the CAR design by reassigning treatment within each bootstrap sample, which causes difficulty in interval estimation under CAR with continuous covariates. We propose a bootstrap method with unequal probability resampling corresponding to the CAR design, avoiding reassignment within each bootstrap sample. In simulations, the proposed CAR methods reduced prognostic imbalance, thereby improving estimation precision compared to existing assignment designs, and the proposed bootstrap method accurately assessed estimation uncertainty under our proposed CAR. An application to Clazosentan trials demonstrated that the proposed CAR methods similarly improved prognostic balance, and the proposed bootstrap method closely reproduced the distribution induced by the proposed CAR.

entry.title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation

link.title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation

entry.content:
Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. NPE’s training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior’s higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.

Read more

entry.title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial

link.title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial

entry.content:
Randomized clinical trials are essential for evaluating interventions, yet average treatment effects can obscure treatment effect heterogeneity, making conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) a natural target. However, restrictive eligibility criteria and differential trial participation can limit the generalizability of these effects to broader target populations. Building on existing DR-Learners, we develop the gDR-Learner for generalizing RCT CATEs to a target population, using cross-fitted machine-learning nuisance estimation. We derive excess-risk bounds in which nuisance errors enter only as products, showing that the estimator achieves oracle-rate convergence despite slower individual nuisance estimation. The variables needed to generalize are rarely measured across the entire target population. We therefore extend the methods to two settings with incomplete covariate information: when certain covariates are measured only in the trial (e.g., biomarkers), and covariates driving trial participation measured only in a subsample of the target population, such as a representative cohort or registry. We construct weighted conformal prediction intervals for individual treatment effects, accounting for covariate shift between the trial and target population. In simulations, the gDR-Learner achieved the lowest estimation error when all covariates were observed relative to standard T- and DR-Learners and an inverse-probability-weighted T-Learner, and also outperformed the latter under incomplete covariate observation. We illustrate the methods by reanalyzing the Coronary Artery Surgery Study, examining treatment effect heterogeneity by prior myocardial infarction and baseline ejection fraction.

entry.title: Data Sketching and Stacking: A Confluence of Two Strategies for Predictive Inference in Gaussian Process Regressions with High-Dimensional Features

link.title: Data Sketching and Stacking: A Confluence of Two Strategies for Predictive Inference in Gaussian Process Regressions with High-Dimensional Features

entry.content:
This article focuses on drawing computationally-efficient predictive inference from Gaussian process (GP) regressions with a large number of features when the response is conditionally independent of the features given the projection to a noisy low dimensional manifold. Bayesian estimation of the regression relationship using Markov Chain Monte Carlo and subsequent predictive inference is computationally prohibitive and may lead to inferential inaccuracies since accurate variable selection is essentially impossible in such high-dimensional GP regressions. As an alternative, this article proposes a strategy to sketch the high-dimensional feature vector with a carefully constructed sketching matrix, before fitting a GP with the scalar outcome and the sketched feature vector to draw predictive inference. The analysis is performed in parallel with many different sketching matrices and smoothing parameters in different processors, and the predictive inferences are combined using Bayesian predictive stacking. Since posterior predictive distribution in each processor is analytically tractable, the algorithm allows bypassing the robustness issues due to convergence and mixing of MCMC chains, leading to fast implementation with very large number of features. Simulation studies show superior performance of the proposed approach with a wide variety of competitors. The approach outperforms competitors in drawing point prediction with predictive uncertainties of outdoor air pollution from satellite images.

Read more

entry.title: Decision-Target Reversal under Informative Label Missingness

link.title: Decision-Target Reversal under Informative Label Missingness

entry.content:
Informative label missingness can improve classification efficiency because the pattern of label availability may itself contain information about the discriminant structure. We show that this advantage need not persist across deployment objectives: with the data-generating model and statistical experiments held fixed, informative partial classification can be favourable under one loss and unfavourable under another. We call this phenomenon decision-target reversal. For binary Gaussian discrimination, we derive a local cost-sensitive excess-risk expansion and, in one dimension, obtain explicit critical cost ratios at which the first-order risk ordering reverses. We show that the required covariance geometry arises under finite uncertainty-dependent missingness mechanisms with a fixed marginal missing-label proportion. We then extend the analysis to multiclass finite-action problems through loss-specific active-boundary curvature, yielding a general decision-target frontier. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate the predicted reversals, and a descriptive gastrointestinal-lesion application with agreement-defined label availability illustrates sensitivity to deployment costs. The results show that favourable informative missingness is a property of the statistical experiment relative to the deployment decision, rather than of the experiment alone.

entry.title: Deep Stochastic Residual Methods for Fully Nonlinear Parabolic Equations

link.title: Deep Stochastic Residual Methods for Fully Nonlinear Parabolic Equations

entry.content:
We develop and analyze neural stochastic residual methods for fully nonlinear parabolic terminal problems under exact diffusion sampling. A quadratic stochastic residual supports global training and backward regression with scalar networks and losses involving only spatial derivatives. For global training, the correction removes a Hessian penalty from the limiting first-order loss. Under a uniform output regularity budget, we bound the continuous residual norm by the square roots of the global loss or normalized backward-regression excess loss, an $O(h^{1/2})$ discretization term for time step $h$, and terminal error. Residual stability then gives value, gradient and Hessian error bounds. Under suitable solution and terminal assumptions, we construct admissible networks with $O(h^{1/2})$ bounds on these approximation errors and the square roots of both loss criteria. In ten-dimensional backward-regression tests using a shared schedule tuned for the quadratic residual, mean relative Hessian errors are $5$–$6\%$ with the quadratic residual and about $15\%$ with the first-order residual. Tuned backward regression achieves Hessian accuracy comparable to physics-informed neural networks across the tested nonlinear coefficients. Translation tests show that the ratio of Hessian error to residual can grow sharply under a fixed sampling law.

Read more

entry.title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference

link.title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference

entry.content:
Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) expands the representational capacity of variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) remains challenging because the marginal score of the semi-implicit distribution is generally intractable. Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) and related methods address this difficulty through reparameterized ELBO gradients, but existing approaches estimate the required score indirectly through reverse-conditional sampling or approximation, which can be computationally costly and unstable. We propose Denoising Implicit Variational Inference (DIVI), which learns the marginal score directly via denoising score matching. The learned score is used as a plug-in estimator in the pathwise ELBO gradient, replacing inner reverse-conditional sampling with a score-network evaluation. We analyze DIVI as inexact stochastic gradient ascent and show, under stated assumptions, that the averaged stationarity measure is controlled by the usual optimization term and the average score-matching error. Empirically, we evaluate DIVI on both synthetic distributions and a variety of real-data Bayesian inference tasks. The results show that DIVI improves over the current UIVI baselines while reducing the cost of ELBO-gradient estimation.

Read more

entry.title: Depth based on translates of a convex body: geometry, floating bodies, and empirical theory

link.title: Depth based on translates of a convex body: geometry, floating bodies, and empirical theory

entry.content:
For a fixed full-dimensional convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, we study the $K$-depth of a point $y$ with respect to a probability measure $\mu$ by comparing the masses of translates of $K$ that fail to contain $y$. Its upper level sets are intersections of high-mass translates of $K$, and hence are convex and admit an exact representation as Minkowski erosions. We distinguish the closed core determined by the maximisers of the translation-mass function from the effective support on which the depth exceeds its unavoidable baseline. We establish continuity, affine equivariance, comparison with halfspace (Tukey) depth, and normal-cone and smoothness criteria. For uniform measures on convex bodies, the regions coincide exactly with the ball floating bodies of Sch"utt, Werner and Yalikun; for positive continuous densities they coincide with the weighted ball floating bodies of Werner and Yalikun. For dilates $tK$, the depth converges to a depth generated by the tangent cones of $K$ as $t \to \infty$; for smooth $K$ this limit is Tukey’s halfspace depth, whereas nonsmooth testing bodies can produce a genuinely different limit. The worst-case maximal $K$-depth is exactly $1/h_T(K)$, where $h_T(K)$ is the Helly number of the family of translates of $K$. Under a uniform interior rolling-ball condition and compact support and having zero mass on hyperplanes, the convergence to halfspace depth is monotone and uniform with an explicit error bound. If the density is bounded by $L$, then this bound is of order $O(t^{-1})$ and this order is sharp. We also record that the dependence on the testing body is not monotone in general, while Hausdorff perturbations of $K$ give stable depth functions and regions at regular levels. Finally, we prove uniform consistency and pointwise weak limits for empirical $K$-depth, including the non-Gaussian limit caused by nonunique active translates.

Read more

entry.title: Detecting acceleration in global mean temperature using supralinear trends

link.title: Detecting acceleration in global mean temperature using supralinear trends

entry.content:
Whether global mean surface temperature has accelerated has received opposite answers in quick succession, reported as undetectable on data to 2023 and as significant on data to 2024. This raises two questions: since when is acceleration detectable, and how far does the answer depend on the test used? We show that structural-break tests, often used for this purpose, cannot reliably date the onset of a continuously accelerating warming rate. We therefore test for curvature directly, under specifications whose null is exactly a constant warming rate and whose alternative is curvature rather than a break. One is a linearithmic trend, which grows faster than linear but more slowly than any polynomial of degree greater than one; the other estimates the curvature freely from the data. We report alongside them the quadratic trend used in the recent literature. Over 1970-2025, in a single full-sample test, the linearithmic and quadratic coefficients are positive and statistically significant in all five major temperature datasets once El Ni~no and solar variability are controlled for. The onset of acceleration is dated by re-estimating over expanding windows and correcting for multiple testing. Under the linearithmic specification, acceleration first becomes detectable in windows ending in mid-2023 for NOAA, late 2023 for GISTEMP and mid-2024 for ERA5, and not yet in HadCRUT or Berkeley. The free-curvature specification agrees on direction but rejects in fewer datasets, since estimating the shape costs precision. The linearithmic specification implies the least curvature of the three, with an acceleration that declines over time, and so the lowest warming of the three when extended to 2050.

Read more

entry.title: Detection Augmented Learning In Non-Stationary Bandit Environments

link.title: Detection Augmented Learning In Non-Stationary Bandit Environments

entry.content:
We study the problem of non-stationary bandits without knowledge of the environmental changes. We propose Detection Augmented Learning (DAL) a black-box paradigm that comprises three modular components: a bandit algorithm, a change detector, and a forced exploration schedule. This modular design enables its applicability across a broad spectrum of bandit problems, from classical to highly structured settings. First, we provide theoretical insights into DAL’s strong empirical performance: a single regret bound shows that DAL transfers the regret of its stationary input to the piecewise stationary setting, attaining or improving the best known bounds in every setting considered. We further identify conditions under which DAL performs well in drifting environments. Then, we showcase DAL’s practical performance and versatility through extensive experimentation in which DAL consistently surpasses all state-of-the-art methods, both prior-free and prior-based, across diverse non-stationary scenarios in nine bandit settings. Finally, we investigate the effectiveness of the forced exploration and show that a bandit-driven strategy improves performance and shortens detection delay.

Read more

entry.title: Dimension-free comparison inequalities between $f$-divergences for Gaussian location mixtures

link.title: Dimension-free comparison inequalities between $f$-divergences for Gaussian location mixtures

entry.content:
We establish dimension-free comparison inequalities between the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and $\chi^2$-divergences and the squared Hellinger distance for Gaussian location mixtures with compactly supported mixing distributions. We show that both divergences are bounded by the squared Hellinger distance up to constants depending only on the radius of the support, independently of the ambient dimension and the number of mixture components. These results resolve an open question raised by \cite{jia2023entropic} and strengthen existing comparison inequalities. Our proof relies on a Gaussian interpolation argument that relates the derivatives of these divergences to differences between posterior means.

entry.title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests

link.title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests

entry.content:
Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with a separate ensemble of treatment trees. The prior on the leaf values of the treatment trees determines whether sampling variability is attributed to the treatment effect. Independent shrinkage priors exert no control over how a tree allocates variability across its leaves, and their total prior variance grows as leaves are added. We propose the Dirichlet-Tree Bayesian Causal Forest, which jointly regularizes the leaf values of each treatment tree through a Dirichlet-Tree prior on their variance shares, generated by stick-breaking along the tree topology. We characterize the spike and tails of the marginal leaf prior, show that the prior adaptively bounds the number of regions of effect heterogeneity, and establish posterior consistency for the forest. In simulations, the model outperforms BCF when heterogeneity is confined to a few regions and reduces spurious heterogeneity elsewhere, and, unlike independent shrinkage priors, its accuracy does not deteriorate as the trees grow. We also evaluate the model on real data, including a pancreatic cancer survival study.

Read more

entry.title: Distinguishability of causal structures under latent confounding and selection

link.title: Distinguishability of causal structures under latent confounding and selection

entry.content:
Statistical relationships in observed data can arise for several different reasons: the observed variables may be causally related, they may share a latent common cause, or there may be selection bias. Each of these scenarios can be modelled using different causal graphs. Not all such causal graphs, however, can be distinguished by experimental data. In this paper, we formulate the equivalence class of causal graphs as a novel graphical structure, the selected-marginalized directed graph (smDG). That is, we show that two directed acyclic graphs with latent and selected vertices have the same smDG if and only if they are indistinguishable, even when allowing for arbitrary interventions on the observed variables. As a substitute for the more familiar d-separation criterion for DAGs, we provide an analogous sound and complete separation criterion in smDGs for conditional independence relative to passive observations. Finally, we provide a series of sufficient conditions under which two causal structures are indistinguishable when there is only access to passive observations.

Read more

entry.title: Divergence based Ranked Preference Alignment for LLMs

link.title: Divergence based Ranked Preference Alignment for LLMs

entry.content:
Alignment of large language models typically relies on pairwise preference feedback, though ranked feedback can capture more comprehensive information across multiple responses within a single annotation. However, ranked-preference alignment is underexplored in practice compared to simpler pairwise approaches, potentially resulting in suboptimal behavior. Concurrently, recent research has conceptualized large language model alignment objectives as divergence estimators between aligned (preferred) and unaligned (less-preferred) response distributions, resulting in a family of objectives with an interpretable theoretical foundation and strong empirical performance. This work unifies these perspectives by introducing $f$-RPO, a $f$-divergence objective for ranked preference optimization that extends divergence-based alignment to ranked feedback and recovers pairwise preference alignment as a special case. Our theoretical analysis establishes rank-order consistency, showing that $f$-RPO preserves the underlying preference ordering at convergence. Empirical results indicate that total-variation and reverse-KL variants of the proposed objective consistently outperform ranked-alignment baselines in both ranking and generation quality across Qwen, Llama, & Gemma models ranging from 0.5B to 8B parameters.

Read more

entry.title: Diversity-Aware Active Learning Builds Materials Datasets for Current and Future Objectives

link.title: Diversity-Aware Active Learning Builds Materials Datasets for Current and Future Objectives

entry.content:
Materials science data collection can be expensive, making dataset reuse and long-term utility important for future discovery. In practice, data collection often prioritizes properties of current interest while other properties are excluded from the acquisition process. This can produce datasets that are well suited for current objectives but lose information needed for properties of future interest. Here, we present how to construct datasets that remain informative for both. We develop and evaluate acquisition frameworks that combine predictive disagreement with diversity in material features, predicted outcomes, or both. We test these approaches across four DFT datasets and an experimental thermoelectric dataset. Diversity inclusion in dataset construction can reduce present and future objectives trade-off by preserving a broader range of materials and property behavior during acquisition. Across all datasets, the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II with disagreements and feature diversity (NSGA-II Dis. + diversity) framework developed in this work provides the most robust balance between current and future objectives. It maintains prediction performance above random sampling for current objectives while mitigating bias on excluded properties and, in many cases, improving their performance beyond random sampling. This diversity-aware acquisition framework provides a practical route to building materials datasets with unbiased quality entries and mitigating cold-start limitations in subsequent modeling and discovery campaigns.

entry.title: Dynamic Prediction of Joint Longitudinal-Survival Models Using a Similarity-Based Approach

link.title: Dynamic Prediction of Joint Longitudinal-Survival Models Using a Similarity-Based Approach

entry.content:
Longitudinal and time-to-event data are often analyzed in biomarker research to study the association between the longitudinal biomarker measurements and the event-time outcome, in which the longitudinal information contributes to the probability of the outcome of interest. An attractive nature of fitting a joint model on this type of data is that we can dynamically predict the survival probability as additional longitudinal information becomes available. We propose a new similarity-based method for the dynamic prediction of joint models where we consider training the model on only a targeted subset of the data to obtain an improved outcome prediction. Through comprehensive simulation study and an application to intensive care unit data, we demonstrate that the predictive performance of the dynamic prediction of joint models can be improved with our proposed similarity-based approach.

entry.title: Efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence

link.title: Efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence

entry.content:
Measures of functional dependence that characterize both independence and perfect dependence have attracted growing interest. Despite their appealing theoretical properties, existing rank- and graph-based estimators can suffer from substantial bias under general dependence, limiting their usefulness for statistical inference. Moreover, a systematic and practically accessible framework for mitigating such bias while achieving semiparametric efficiency remains largely unavailable. In this paper, we develop a general framework for efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence through sample-splitting and cross-fitting. Our approach enables systematic bias reduction and semiparametrically efficient inference, and thus offers a flexible and theoretically grounded alternative to existing rank- and graph-based methods.

Read more

entry.title: Enhancing Offline Model-Based RL via Active Model Selection: A Bayesian Optimization Perspective

link.title: Enhancing Offline Model-Based RL via Active Model Selection: A Bayesian Optimization Perspective

entry.content:
Offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) serves as a competitive framework that can learn well-performing policies solely from pre-collected data with the help of learned dynamics models. To fully unleash the power of offline MBRL, model selection plays a pivotal role in determining the dynamics model utilized for downstream policy learning. However, offline MBRL conventionally relies on validation or off-policy evaluation, which are rather inaccurate due to the inherent distribution shift in offline RL. To tackle this, we propose BOMS, an active model selection framework that enhances model selection in offline MBRL with only a small online interaction budget, through the lens of Bayesian optimization (BO). Specifically, we recast model selection as BO and enable probabilistic inference in BOMS by proposing a novel model-induced kernel, which is theoretically grounded and computationally efficient. Through extensive experiments, we show that BOMS improves over the baseline methods with a small amount of online interaction comparable to only $1\%$-$2.5\%$ of offline training data on various RL tasks.

Read more

entry.title: Ensemble Control Variates

link.title: Ensemble Control Variates

entry.content:
Control variates have become an increasingly popular variance-reduction technique in Bayesian inference. Many broadly applicable control variates are based on the Langevin-Stein operator, which leverages gradient information available from gradient-based samplers to produce variance-reduced estimators of expectations. These control variates typically require optimising over a function $u(\theta)$ within a user-defined functional class $\mathcal{G}$, such as the space of $Q$th-order polynomials or a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We propose using averaging-based ensemble learning to construct Stein-based control variates. While the proposed framework is broadly applicable, we focus on ensembles constructed from zero-variance control variates (ZVCV), a popular parametric approach based on solving a linear approximation problem that can easily be over-parameterised in medium-to-high dimensional settings. A common remedy is to use regularised ZVCV via penalised regression, but these methods can be prohibitively slow. We introduce ensemble ZVCV methods based on ensembles of OLS estimators and evaluate the proposed methods against established methods in the literature in a simulation study. Our results show that ensemble ZVCV methods are more statistically efficient than regularised ZVCV methods, while also being substantially faster. This work opens a new direction for constructing broadly applicable control variate techniques via ensemble learning.

Read more

entry.title: Ergodic Central limit theorem for subgeometric Markov chains

link.title: Ergodic Central limit theorem for subgeometric Markov chains

entry.content:
We establish verifiable necessary conditions for central limit theorems (CLTs) of ergodic averages of Markov chains on general state spaces. Our criteria are based on discrete-time $\mathbf{L}$-drift conditions that can be verified through estimates for the one-step transition kernel of the original chain. They yield an integral criterion for failure of the CLT for a class of observables that includes unbounded functions and indicators of tail events. The main technical step transfers lower bounds for excursions of the original chain to regenerative excursions of its Nummelin split chain. The same drift conditions yield lower bounds on the tails of return times and modulated excursion functionals, on invariant tails, and on rates of convergence in $f$-variation and $L^p$-Wasserstein distance. These estimates apply without an explicit formula for the invariant distribution. Applications to unadjusted Langevin algorithms show preservation of polynomial target tail indices at every fixed step size. For Euler schemes with additive infinite-variance noise, we establish restrictions on invariant tails and transience under superlinear drifts. Schemes with linear drift, multiplicative noise and logarithmic innovation tails exhibit sharp polynomial convergence exponents and exact CLT thresholds, despite the absence of positive Euclidean moments.

Read more

entry.title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models

link.title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models

entry.content:
Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.

Read more

entry.title: Estimating treatment effects with a unified semi-parametric difference-in-differences approach

link.title: Estimating treatment effects with a unified semi-parametric difference-in-differences approach

entry.content:
Difference-in-differences (DID) approaches estimate causal effects with observational data before and after an intervention. DID traditionally estimates the average treatment effect among the treated and assumes parallel trends in outcome means. With skewed outcomes, a transformation is often needed to compare means; however, transformations may be difficult to choose and results may be sensitive to the choice and must be interpreted on the transformed scale. Recent DID methods estimate alternative treatment effects that offer additional insights. However, each estimator requires a different parallel trends assumption. We introduce a new DID method that estimates average, quantile, probability, and novel Mann-Whitney treatment effects among the treated with a single unifying parallel trends assumption. The method uses a semi-parametric cumulative probability model (CPM): a linear model for a latent variable on covariates, where the latent variable results from an unspecified transformation of the outcome. Our approach makes a single parallel trends assumption on the expectation of the latent variable conditional on covariates. Hence, we avoid specifying outcome transformations and separate estimand-specific assumptions. We introduce the method; describe identification, estimation, and inference; conduct simulations evaluating its performance; and apply it to assess the impact of Medicaid expansion on CD4 count among people with HIV.

Read more

entry.title: Estimation and Inference for the Joint Autoregressive Quantile-Expected Shortfall Model

link.title: Estimation and Inference for the Joint Autoregressive Quantile-Expected Shortfall Model

entry.content:
Expected shortfall is defined as the truncated mean of a random variable that falls below a specified quantile level and is widely recognized as an important risk measure. Motivated by the empirical observation of clustering patterns in financial risks, we consider a joint autoregressive model for both conditional quantile and expected shortfall. Existing estimation methods for such models typically rely on minimizing a nonlinear and nonconvex joint loss function, which is challenging to solve. We introduce a two-step regression framework to estimate the model parameters with theoretical guarantees. We further develop a Portmanteau test for model diagnostics and prove its asymptotic validity for Type I error control. Our empirical results on stock market data indicate that the proposed models effectively capture the clustering patterns and leverage effects on the conditional expected shortfall.

Read more

entry.title: Exploiting sparse conditional dependence in remote sensing observing systems

link.title: Exploiting sparse conditional dependence in remote sensing observing systems

entry.content:
We develop a novel filtering algorithm for remote sensing inverse problems that exploits sparsity in the precision (inverse covariance) matrix arising from conditional independence structures in spatio-temporal satellite data. Motivated by NASA’s Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2), Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT), and upcoming Explorer for Artemis Geology Lunar and Earth (EAGLE) missions, we formulate a Bayesian inference framework for retrieving atmospheric and surface parameters from hyperspectral radiance measurements. Unlike traditional methods that operate on covariances and ignore spatio-temporal dependencies, our approach models the full spatio-temporal state using sparse Gaussian graphical models, which corresponds to a block-sparse precision matrix. We derive an information filter based on this structure, enabling scalable joint inference over large spatial grids with uncertainty propagation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm in two distinct remote sensing contexts. First, we apply the method to synthetic data configured to mimic the OCO-2 mission, focusing on retrievals of atmospheric CO$_2$, and observe a 50% reduction in CO$_2$ retrieval error compared to single-pixel methods. Then, we evaluate the algorithm using imaging spectroscopy data from the Surface Biology and Geology (SBG) High Frequency Time Series (SHIFT) campaign to retrieve surface reflectance, achieving a 20% reduction in retrieval error relative to baseline approaches.

Read more

entry.title: Extrinsic MANOVA for Oriented Projective Shapes

link.title: Extrinsic MANOVA for Oriented Projective Shapes

entry.content:
For configurations of landmarks reconstructed from camera images, classical projective shape analysis identifies antipodal spherical representatives of projective coordinates, while oriented projective shape (OPS) retains their distinction. In 3D, a fixed oriented-projective coordinate representation of a OPS is point on product of 3D spheres. We develop nonparametric multisample inference for equality of population extrinsic means on this product. Quaternion multiplication helps create a global orthonormal tangent frame field, in which we obtain explicit extrinsic covariance blocks that preserve dependence between registered landmarks. A covariance-weighted MANOVA statistic has a chi-square null limit under nonfocality of distributions and positive-definite extrinsic covariance assumptions. An inverse-free discrepancy has a weighted chi-square limit when covariance matrices may be singular, and centered, groupwise nonparametric bootstrap procedures are justified asymptotically. We apply a fixed-observed-covariance nonparametric bootstrap version of the weighted statistic to 31 seven-landmark facial reconstructions from five subjects. Separate tests at the right inner brow and chin reject equality of the five OPS mean directions after Bonferroni adjustment. The analysis concerns a common mixed-sign frame domain and marginal landmarks; it does not establish pairwise subject differences or a joint six-dimensional facial test.

Read more

entry.title: FairBED: Incorporating Fairness into Bayesian Experimental Design

link.title: FairBED: Incorporating Fairness into Bayesian Experimental Design

entry.content:
Bayesian experimental design (BED) has traditionally focused exclusively on collecting data that is maximally informative, with little consideration of other desirable dataset characteristics, such as fairness. We therefore extend BED to target data that is both informative and fair. To this end, we introduce FairBED, which provides a formalism for the fairness of datasets themselves by measuring how compatible they are with a fair world, in which the target quantity we wish to learn about is unrelated to the sensitive attributes we want to be fair to. We then use this to construct practical fairness-aware BED objectives that maximise expected information gain about the target variables, while penalising information about sensitive attributes and/or their coupling with the target. We further extend FairBED to active learning, and show empirically that models trained on data gathered using FairBED provide improved fairness-accuracy trade-offs compared to randomly acquired data and conventional BED.

Read more

entry.title: Fair Regression under Approximate Demographic Parity

link.title: Fair Regression under Approximate Demographic Parity

entry.content:
Exact demographic parity requires the same prediction distribution across sensitive groups. In regression, this can be too restrictive and reduce predictive accuracy. We instead bound every pairwise Wasserstein distance between group-specific prediction distributions by a chosen tolerance, allowing the groups to differ while keeping fairness tunable. On the real line, the prediction and constrained transport problems have the same infimum. If the transport problem attains this value and suitable Monge maps exist, a deterministic transport-form predictor realizes it. Under a standard one-dimensional condition, the problem becomes a bounded quantile optimization that is convex when the conditional expected loss is convex in prediction. Under squared loss with two positively weighted groups, the $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_\infty$ constraints yield soft-thresholding, shrinkage, and clipping. Under the stated conditions, we establish rates for the known-cost plug-in estimator. When the cost is unavailable, we describe an observed-loss computational proxy. Synthetic and California 2018 ACS studies illustrate the tunable fairness-accuracy trade-off and distinguish calibration feasibility from held-out fairness and accuracy.

Read more

entry.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks

link.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks

entry.content:
We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.94 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

Read more

entry.title: Federated Learning: From Theory to Practice

link.title: Federated Learning: From Theory to Practice

entry.content:
This book offers a hands-on introduction to building and understanding federated learning (FL) systems. FL enables multiple devices – such as smartphones, sensors, or local computers – to collaboratively train machine learning (ML) models, while keeping their data private and local. It is a powerful solution when data cannot or should not be centralized due to privacy, regulatory, or technical reasons. The book is designed for students, engineers, and researchers who want to learn how to design scalable, privacy preserving FL systems. Our main focus is on personalization: enabling each device to train its own model while still benefiting from collaboration with relevant devices. This is achieved by leveraging similarities between (the learning tasks associated with) devices that are encoded by the weighted edges (or links) of a federated learning network (FL network). The key idea is to represent real-world FL systems as networks of devices, where nodes correspond to device and edges represent communication links and data similarities between them. The training of personalized models for these devices can be naturally framed as a distributed optimization problem. This optimization problem is referred to as generalized total variation minimization (GTVMin) and ensures that devices with similar learning tasks learn similar model parameters. Our approach is both mathematically principled and practically motivated. While we introduce some advanced ideas from optimization theory and graph-based learning, we aim to keep the book accessible. Readers are guided through the core ideas step by step, with intuitive explanations.

Read more

entry.title: Financial Literacy and the Functional Shape of Subjective Time Deformation in Intertemporal Choice

link.title: Financial Literacy and the Functional Shape of Subjective Time Deformation in Intertemporal Choice

entry.content:
Intertemporal decisions are commonly summarized by a single discount parameter, although individuals with similar overall discounting intensity may value short-, medium-, and long-term delays differently. This study investigates whether financial literacy is associated with these horizon-specific differences by treating reconstructed subjective time as a functional rather than scalar outcome. Data were collected through a multilingual online questionnaire administered to a convenience and snowball sample of 140 adults, who provided hypothetical equivalence judgments for a future reward of EUR 100 over 13 horizons from 7 days to 5 years, a three-item financial-literacy measure, and measures of temporal perception. Individual discount trajectories were reconstructed and analyzed with function-on-scalar regression, allowing the association with financial literacy to vary across the temporal domain. Because the normalized subjective-time trajectory is not identifiable for flat or reconstruction-degenerate discount profiles, the primary functional analysis included 59 participants, while complementary analyses used the full analytical sample. The primary model provided no evidence of a robust linear association between financial literacy and subjective-time deformation. An exploratory categorical specification indicated heterogeneity across financial-literacy levels and departure from a linear-score representation, although individual contrasts were imprecise and sensitive to specification. The relationship between financial literacy and intertemporal valuation may thus be more complex than a monotonic score effect, and functional data analytics can reveal horizon-specific structure that scalar summaries obscure. Given the convenience sample and the reduced identified sample, the results are exploratory and require validation in larger independent samples.

Read more

entry.title: Gaussian Process Bandits with Paired Auxiliary Observations

link.title: Gaussian Process Bandits with Paired Auxiliary Observations

entry.content:
Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet observation noise makes each evaluation less informative and slows posterior learning. Standard BO learns from costly outcomes gathered during optimization. In many applications, however, low-cost auxiliary data are available beforehand. We introduce Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (AI-GPB), a variance-reduction method that combines an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. Notably, it exploits correlation between paired observation errors without requiring the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. We establish finite-sample GP confidence bounds and regret guarantees, including explicit cumulative and simple regret rates for Mat'ern kernels. Numerical experiments across continuous BO benchmarks with varied landscapes and dimensions show consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla GP-UCB, even when within-pair correlation is moderate and the auxiliary mean is estimated from noisy offline data.

Read more

author.name: Weibo Huang, Qing Feng, Ruihao Zhu, Cheng Hua

entry.summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet observation noise makes each evaluation less informative and slows posterior learning. Standard BO learns from costly outcomes gathered during optimization. In many applications, however, low-cost auxiliary data are available beforehand. We introduce Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (AI-GPB), a variance-reduction method that combines an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. Notably, it exploits correlation between paired observation errors without requiring the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. We establish finite-sample GP confidence bounds and regret guarantees, including explicit cumulative and simple regret rates for Mat'ern kernels. Numerical experiments across continuous BO benchmarks with varied landscapes and dimensions show consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla GP-UCB, even when within-pair correlation is moderate and the auxiliary mean is estimated from noisy offline data.

entry.title: Generative Flows for Potential Outcomes and Counterfactuals

link.title: Generative Flows for Potential Outcomes and Counterfactuals

entry.content:
Average treatment effects summarize how interventions change outcomes, but individualized decisions require predictions and outcome distributions of what would have happened to the same individual under an alternative treatment. We develop PO-Flow, a continuous normalizing flow framework that represents treatment-specific outcome distributions through invertible transport maps. It supports potential-outcome generation, conditional average treatment-effect estimation, factual-conditioned counterfactual prediction, and density evaluation. To address treatment imbalance in observational data, we incorporate cross-fitted inverse-probability weighting into the flow-matching loss. We establish sufficient conditions under which encoding a factual outcome and decoding under an alternative treatment recovers the individual counterfactual. Under shared exogenous noise and a common encoded reference distribution, scalar recovery follows from increasing noise-to-latent maps. For multivariate outcomes, we assume triangularity or a convex-gradient structure. These conditions distinguish fitting outcome distributions from recovering their causal correspondence. Experiments on four scalar benchmarks and seven multivariate or image settings, with dimensions up to 784, compare against ten scalar and five multivariate baselines. Controlled ablations show IPW improves all reported scalar counterfactual RMSE, PEHE, and potential-outcome RMSE. PO-Flow achieves the lowest PEHE and potential-outcome RMSE on all four scalar benchmarks and attains or ties the lowest mean in 26 of 35 multivariate dataset–metric comparisons.

entry.title: Geometry-Adaptive Clustering on High-Dimensional Tori

link.title: Geometry-Adaptive Clustering on High-Dimensional Tori

entry.content:
Multivariate angular data lie on a torus, but clustering methods often use the flat torus. We introduce curved-torus energy (CTE), a position-dependent dissimilarity based on restricted Riemannian path energy and minimization over winding classes. CTE has a certified finite winding reduction, an exact flat endpoint, a geodesic upper bound, and stability with respect to the geometry parameter. For label-free geometry selection, we propose CEHS-HM, a held-out criterion for selecting the warping parameter at a specified clustering resolution. We establish a finite-grid population-score regret bound and also consider joint geometry-resolution selection over finite candidate grids. Controlled experiments on $\mathbb{T}^3$ show that CTE agrees with the flat method at zero warping and becomes more useful as geometric warping increases. Additional experiments show that the CEHS-selected geometry should be viewed as a data-adaptive clustering choice rather than as an estimator of a generative deformation parameter. Under a product-von-Mises mechanism, the selector tends toward the flat endpoint when curvature is unnecessary. On ILE protein torsion data, the proposed method identifies a stable five-mode representation of joint backbone-side-chain conformation.

Read more

entry.title: Granular Instrumental Variables in Large Panels: Identification and Inference Across Strong, Nearly Weak, and Weak GIV

link.title: Granular Instrumental Variables in Large Panels: Identification and Inference Across Strong, Nearly Weak, and Weak GIV

entry.content:
Granular Instrumental Variables (GIV), introduced by Gabaix and Koijen (2024), use idiosyncratic shocks to large units as instruments for aggregate endogenous variables. I develop asymptotic theory for GIV in large panels where both the cross section and time series grow ((N,T\to\infty)). I make two main contributions. First, I show that estimating the individual shocks used to construct the granular instrument has a first-order effect on the asymptotic variance of the GIV estimator. Existing methods do not account for this effect, leading to incorrect standard errors. I derive corrected inference. Second, I characterize how instrument strength changes as (N) grows, yielding strong, nearly-weak, and weak regimes. In the newly characterized nearly-weak regime, the instrument vanishes asymptotically but the estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal, at a slower rate, when (T) grows sufficiently fast relative to (N). I apply the theory to estimate short-run supply and demand elasticities for crude oil, copper, and natural gas.

Read more

entry.title: Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control for Stable Counterfactual Estimation under Donor Redundancy

link.title: Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control for Stable Counterfactual Estimation under Donor Redundancy

entry.content:
Synthetic control methods estimate counterfactual outcomes by weighting untreated donor units to match a treated unit before treatment. In recent applications, however, the donor pool can be large, highly correlated, and short in pre-treatment history, yielding many near-equivalent solutions with unstable and difficult-to-interpret donor weights. We propose Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control (Graph-SC), a convex estimator that augments the classical pre-treatment matching objective with a graph Laplacian penalty. The graph encodes similarity among donor trajectories, encouraging coherent weights over structurally related donors while preserving the transparency of synthetic controls. We provide theoretical results characterizing the bias-variance tradeoff induced by graph regularization and establish efficient convergence guarantees with an accelerated proximal gradient method. Across a controlled simulation under donor redundancy, the California Proposition 99 benchmark, and observational counterfactual analyses on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, Graph-SC improves weight stability, reduces sensitivity to redundant donor pools, and maintains competitive pre- and post-treatment accuracy relative to classical and regularized synthetic control baselines. Our results suggest that graph regularization is most valuable not as a universal accuracy booster, but as a principled mechanism for selecting stable and interpretable counterfactuals from near-equivalent synthetic controls with comparable pre-treatment fit.

entry.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

link.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

entry.content:
Regression-based survey weighting connects model-based population estimation with design-based inference through equivalent weights. For nonlinear models, equivalent weights can be defined locally through the sensitivity of a poststratified population estimator. However, conventional regression models may inadequately capture nonlinear relationships and complex interactions across sparse poststratification cells. We develop a survey-weighting framework based on hierarchical Gaussian process (HGP) regression, combining structured group-level effects with kernel-based smoothing to share information across related cells. We derive Gaussian posterior prediction formulas that exploit the structured covariance representation to reduce computational costs. We also establish a uniform convergence result for the posterior predictive mean under stated regularity conditions and construct local equivalent weights by matching the first-order sensitivity of a plug-in poststratified estimand to that of a weighted average of fitted response means, with both derivatives taken with respect to the latent mean-scale vector. Simulations show that HGP achieves lower population-weighted prediction error under nonparametric structure, whereas logistic regression performs well under correct parametric specification. Additional analyses examine sample size, frame coverage, subgroup prediction, and population-mean agreement. An application to the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study illustrates the method. Overall, this work extends local equivalent-weight construction to nonparametric modeling and provides a computational framework and conditional theoretical results for survey weighting in structured, sparse populations.

Read more

entry.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

link.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

entry.content:
Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett–Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph’s connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.

Read more

entry.title: Higher Order Risk Comparisons of Oracle Calibrated Global Local Priors

link.title: Higher Order Risk Comparisons of Oracle Calibrated Global Local Priors

entry.content:
First-order minimaxity offers limited guidance for choosing among global-local shrinkage priors, since different local-tail distributions can yield the same leading risk. Comparisons at a common global scale may also be misleading, as the scale interacts with the shape of the local prior. We study the worst-case squared-error risks of posterior means in sparse Gaussian normal-means estimation, allowing each prior its own risk-minimizing global scale. For local-variance priors with polynomial tails and logarithmic corrections, we characterize the calibrations that retain first- and second-order minimaxity and derive the asymptotic form of the unrestricted oracle scale. Even after this optimization, differences in risk remain. The polynomial tail index, logarithmic tail exponent and a scale-invariant higher-order correction distinguish priors at successively finer orders. In particular, the horseshoe has smaller asymptotic oracle risk than the horseshoe+, despite the latter’s additional logarithmic tail factor. We also establish the calibration accuracy needed to preserve these differences and sufficient conditions for their stability under high-dimensional Gaussian regression designs.

Read more

entry.title: Hybrid Topic-Semantic Labeling and Graph Embeddings for Unsupervised Legal Document Clustering

link.title: Hybrid Topic-Semantic Labeling and Graph Embeddings for Unsupervised Legal Document Clustering

entry.content:
Legal documents pose substantial challenges for unsupervised knowledge discovery due to specialized domain terminology, multi-scale document lengths, and scarce expert annotations. This paper introduces Topic-Graph Spherical Fusion (TGSF), a dual-manifold representation learning framework for unsupervised legal document clustering that unifies dense topic-semantic discovery and relational graph embeddings on a joint unit hypersphere. Instantiating dense topic discovery via Top2Vec and biased second-order random walks via Node2Vec, TGSF constructs a connected multi-relational document-topic graph combining multi-topic centroid bridges with temperature-sharpened semantic k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) document edges, guaranteeing a single connected component. The resulting L2-normalized semantic and graph representations are fused via modality-weighted concatenation onto a joint unit hypersphere prior to KMeans partitioning, decomposing squared chordal distance into a convex combination of semantic and structural cosine similarities. Evaluations across three legal benchmarks (ACORD, CUAD, and LEDGAR) show that TGSF outperforms semantic-only, structural-only, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and TF-IDF baselines. Across 216 factorial grid configurations and 240 Bayesian TPE and Multi-Objective NSGA-II Pareto optimization trials per dataset (720 trials total), TGSF improves Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) from 0.606 to 0.653 on LEDGAR (ARI = 0.425), 0.228 to 0.284 on ACORD (ARI = 0.260), and 0.535 to 0.570 on CUAD (ARI = 0.282). Functional ANOVA and Pareto frontier diagnostics further characterize hyperparameter sensitivity for reproducible legal text mining.

entry.title: ICON decomposition: Multivariate concept auditing reveals shortcuts that neural networks rely on

link.title: ICON decomposition: Multivariate concept auditing reveals shortcuts that neural networks rely on

entry.content:
Deep neural networks often exploit spurious associations, a failure known as shortcut learning. Before deployment, models should therefore be audited for reliance on concepts such as acquisition artifacts and patient demographics. Current methods, including linear probes and concept activation vectors, measure concept reliance by asking whether each concept is decodable from a layer. We show that this framing is misleading: decodability reflects not only concept reliance but also correlations among concepts and the outcome in the auditing dataset. We reframe shortcut auditing as a decomposition of the variance of intermediary representations with Independent Canonical cONcepts (ICON). ICON quantifies the share of a layer’s variance explained by each concept conditional on all other concepts and the outcome, and also reports the variance left unexplained. Because ICON explanations are comparable across layers, their trajectories distinguish concepts that drive predictions from those that are merely encoded in the representations. In simulated data with ground truth, ICON recovers concept importance more accurately than seven baselines. In skin-cancer and neuroimaging applications, it separates learned shortcuts from merely correlated concepts, which we confirm with independent validation checks.

Read more

entry.title: Identifying Elasticities in Autocorrelated Time Series Using Causal Mechanism Graphs

link.title: Identifying Elasticities in Autocorrelated Time Series Using Causal Mechanism Graphs

entry.content:
Instrumental variable (IV) methods are widely used to estimate the price elasticity of demand from observational data. However, naive IV estimators may be inconsistent in settings with autocorrelated time series. We argue that causal graphs taking into account time structure can simplify IV identification and help select consistent estimators. More precisely, we propose to model equilibrium conditions using causal mechanism time graphs. These (acyclic) graphs allow us to maintain the assumption of a simultaneous determination of prices and quantities and come with an interpretable notion of intervention. They further allow us to exploit recent advances in graphical inference to derive valid IV estimators that are consistent under weak assumptions. Finally, we argue that observing significant differences between the estimates of presumably valid estimators can help to reject false model assumptions, thereby improving our understanding of underlying economic dynamics. We apply our approach to the German electricity market, estimating the price elasticity of demand from simulated and real-world data. The findings underscore the importance of accounting for structural autocorrelation in IV-based analysis.

entry.title: Incorporating therapist capacity, availability and turnover in trials of therapist-delivered interventions: Non-orthogonal factorial designs

link.title: Incorporating therapist capacity, availability and turnover in trials of therapist-delivered interventions: Non-orthogonal factorial designs

entry.content:
Disentangling therapist from intervention effects has long been considered a challenge in randomised trials of therapist delivered interventions. When separating these effects is of interest, factorial designs have been proposed in which therapists and interventions are regarded as two potentially interacting components of a complex intervention, represented by two treatment factors (one random, one fixed). In these trial designs, every therapist delivers each intervention, and patients are randomised to the resulting therapist intervention combinations. It is assumed that each therapist is allocated the same number of patients (equal capacity), that all therapists in a centre are available when a patient is randomised (equal availability), and that therapists remain involved for the entire duration of the trial (no turnover). In practice, these are strong assumptions that may lead to delayed or suspended randomisation and increased trial costs. We propose three novel randomisation strategies that explicitly account for therapist capacity, availability, and turnover while maintaining desirable statistical properties. In a simulation study, we compared the proposed and existing randomisation strategies across trial scenarios and design parameters, assessing trade offs between operational efficiency and statistical performance. The results provide practical guidance for trialists designing trials of therapist delivered interventions under real world constraints.

entry.title: Interacting Annealed Importance Sampling via Population-Based MCMC Kernels

link.title: Interacting Annealed Importance Sampling via Population-Based MCMC Kernels

entry.content:
Sampling from a multimodal distribution is a fundamental and challenging problem in computational science and statistics. Among various approaches proposed for this task, one popular method is Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS). In this paper, we propose an interaction-based version of AIS by combining it with population-based Monte Carlo methods to improve its efficiency. By keeping track of an ensemble instead of a single sampler along some continuation path between the starting distribution and the target distribution, we take advantage of the interaction within the ensemble to encourage the exploration of undiscovered modes. Specifically, our main idea is to utilize either the snooker algorithm or the genetic algorithm used in Evolutionary Monte Carlo. We discuss how the proposed algorithm can be implemented and derive a partial differential equation governing the evolution of the ensemble under the continuous time and mean-field limit. We also test the efficiency of the proposed algorithm on various continuous and discrete distributions.

entry.title: Interpretable time series analysis with Gumbel dynamics

link.title: Interpretable time series analysis with Gumbel dynamics

entry.content:
Switching dynamical systems can model complicated time series data while maintaining interpretability by inferring a finite set of dynamics primitives and explaining different portions of the observed time series with one of these primitives. However, due to the discrete nature of this set, such models struggle to capture smooth, variable-speed transitions, as well as stochastic mixtures of overlapping states (e.g., non-instantaneous state transitions), and the inferred dynamics often display spurious rapid switching on real-world datasets. Here, we propose the Gumbel Dynamical Model (GDM). First, by introducing a continuous relaxation of discrete states and a different noise model defined on the relaxed-discrete state space via the Gumbel distribution, GDM expands the set of available state dynamics, allowing the model to approximate smoother and non-stationary ground-truth dynamics more faithfully. Breaking from established literature, this new class uses a stochastic relaxed state to directly combine reusable dynamical primitives and govern observations, without a separate stochastic continuous trajectory. Second, the relaxation makes the model fully differentiable, enabling fast and scalable training with standard gradient descent methods. We validate our approach on standard simulation datasets and highlight its ability to model soft, sticky states and transitions in a stochastic setting. Furthermore, we apply our model to two real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to infer interpretable states in stochastic time series with multiple dynamics, a setting where traditional methods often fail.

Furthermore, we apply our model to two real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to infer interpretable states in stochastic time series with multiple dynamics, a setting where traditional methods often fail.

entry.title: Inverse Confounding Analysis: An Exact Method for Quantifying the Significance of Confounding

link.title: Inverse Confounding Analysis: An Exact Method for Quantifying the Significance of Confounding

entry.content:
The presence of unmeasured confounding factors during the collection of observational data may lead to biased estimates of the effect of an exposure on an outcome. Consequently, a central problem in causal inference based on observational data is sensitivity analysis with respect to unmeasured confounding. Existing sensitivity analyses generally focus on worst-case bounds. We propose an exact method for quantifying the significance of confounding, defined here in terms of the complete range of analytical estimates of the stratification-based Risk Ratio over the set of all joint distributions compatible with the observed characteristics. We refer to the proposed method as Inverse Confounding Analysis (ICA). The proposed ICA method extends the widely used E-value approach but, in contrast to it, does not restrict the analysis to a worst-case lower bound. Instead, it provides exact estimates over the entire set of admissible configurations. This requires several additional input parameters, namely the frequencies of the exposure, the confounder, and the outcome. The ICA method is based on an inverse problem: reconstructing the set of admissible joint distributions from specified frequencies and pairwise associations. We formulate this reconstruction problem as a system of nonlinear equations and obtain an analytical solution. Surprisingly, the complete solution set can be parameterized linearly by a single free parameter. The corresponding stratification-based Risk Ratio is then represented as a fractional-linear function of this parameter. This representation makes it possible to derive exact analytical measures of the significance of confounding over the entire set of admissible statistical configurations.

Read more

entry.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding

link.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding

entry.content:
Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder’s own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.

Read more

entry.title: Kriging Beyond Gaussianity: Fixed-Domain Asymptotic Optimality

link.title: Kriging Beyond Gaussianity: Fixed-Domain Asymptotic Optimality

entry.content:
Under squared-error loss, the optimal predictor of a non-Gaussian random field is its conditional mean, which may be difficult to compute. We consider a broad class of non-Gaussian random fields obtained by transforming finitely many independent Gaussian fields sharing a common correlation function, and study when kriging entails no first-order loss in mean squared prediction error (MSPE) under fixed-domain asymptotics. We compare the observed-data conditional mean, kriging with the observed covariance, kriging with the latent correlation, and a latent-information oracle. These predictors satisfy a finite-sample MSPE ordering. Under conditions linking transformation regularity to the high-frequency decay of the latent spectral density, all four MSPEs are asymptotically equivalent. For radially nonincreasing spectral densities with polynomial tails, the required regularity order is independent of both the spatial dimension and the number of latent fields. Exponential correlation also yields finite-sample bounds. Examples include Weibull, skew-Gaussian, and copula-based fields, while numerical comparisons illustrate finite-sample differences. Counterexamples show why covariance structure and first-order transformation regularity alone are insufficient. Finally, standardized prediction errors converge to a Gaussian scale mixture, which is standard normal exactly when the transformation’s gradient norm is almost surely constant.

Read more

entry.title: Learning to Refer: Inference-Time Collaboration in Decentralized Federated Learning

link.title: Learning to Refer: Inference-Time Collaboration in Decentralized Federated Learning

entry.content:
In decentralized federated learning, heterogeneous clients may develop complementary expertise, yet each query is typically evaluated only by the client where it arrives. To exploit this distributed expertise without global coordination, we formulate inference-time collaboration as budgeted local expert referral, a graph-constrained routing process in which a query can move only between neighboring clients and only visited clients contribute to its final prediction. EdgeDRM implements this framework by learning a density-based routing potential for each client: differences between neighboring potentials provide the comparisons used to select successive referrals, while local task models generate predictions that are aggregated along the resulting route. Both training and inference are decentralized, using only neighbor-local information without a central router or graph-wide client scoring. We establish estimation guarantees for the learned comparisons and characterize how local improvement and graph structure govern prior-weighted density gains from referral. Experiments on benchmark and real-world medical data show that EdgeDRM outperforms graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, with the clearest benefits under sparse connectivity.

Read more

entry.title: Load Balancing with Evolving Workloads in Large-Scale Language Model Serving

link.title: Load Balancing with Evolving Workloads in Large-Scale Language Model Serving

entry.content:
Serving large language models requires assigning requests whose workloads grow during processing and whose completion times are unknown. With a synchronization barrier, lightly loaded workers wait for the slowest worker at every decode iteration. We model this loss through aggregate workload imbalance and formulate a joint admission and assignment problem with sticky requests and capacity limits. Short lookahead incorporates predicted completions of ongoing requests. For exact optimization without lookahead, we prove a comparison under independent geometric decode lengths, bounded independent nondegenerate prompt sizes, and batched releases satisfying a cumulative supply condition. The long-run expected imbalance improvement over first come, first served admission with request-count join-shortest-queue grows at least as the square root of the product of worker capacity and the logarithm of worker count, in the stated scaling regime. The comparison extends to capacity-aware round robin, random routing, and power of two choices. BalanceRoute approximations connect the formulation to practical routing. Experiments using up to 144 NPUs with proprietary and public traces show lower workload spread and higher throughput than the evaluated baselines. These empirical results complement the guarantee for exact optimization.

Read more

entry.title: Local Manifold Attention for Recovery and Generation of Rare 3D Human Poses

link.title: Local Manifold Attention for Recovery and Generation of Rare 3D Human Poses

entry.content:
A rare 3D human pose in a motion sequence may reflect either a genuine movement or an estimation error, making correction difficult when reference databases contain few comparable examples. We investigate whether local geometric structure can support the recovery and generation of rare configura- tions, using motion-capture sequences from AMASS, which unifies datasets through a common parametric human-body model, together with video-based pose estimates. We develop the cylindrical manifold attention transformer (CMAT), which extends local manifold fitting through geometry- and task- dependent neighborhood weights. For motion correction, Self-Action CMAT draws on comparable windows within a sequence, adjusts their contributions for neighborhood imbalance and temporal dependence, and integrates local geometry with robust temporal regularization. Experiments on perturbed and estimated motions show reductions in position and acceleration errors, with component analyses examining how weighting and temporal processing con- tribute to recovery. The controlled correction comparisons are exploratory and conditional on the selected motion-amplitude bound. For generation, Rarity-preserving CMAT explores locally supported configurations subject to independently calibrated rarity and separation from stored observations. Under common screening criteria, it achieves a higher yield of eligible rare poses than the evaluated generation baselines.
