entry.title: Local data augmentation for imbalanced binary classification

link.title: Local data augmentation for imbalanced binary classification

entry.content:
Facing imbalanced binary classification, we aim at maximizing the recall while limiting the proportion of false detections in the minority class. For doing that, the present work studies the effect of several rebalancing strategies, from the uniform subsampling of the observations from the minority class, to a more involved local data augmentation scheme. To be more specific, we establish that only rebalancing class proportions cannot modify the classification performance, whereas local data augmentation is proved to have an impact on the final results. The local augmentation scheme is introduced by means of a two-step procedure. The first step randomly subsamples anchor points among the training observations. These anchor points are used in the second step, for drawing new augmentation data following an ‘‘augmentation kernel’’ to be specified. This enables us to decouple the impact of the anchor points subsampling from the one of drawing augmentation data accounting (or not) for the local geometry of the support. The experiments on synthetic data illustrate the practical performance of several strategies for subsampling anchor points combined with either a Gaussian or a diffusion-based augmentation kernel. Compared to SMOTE-like data augmentation procedures, a better performance is achieved when subsampling in the close neighborhood to the classification boundary combined with a Gaussian augmentation kernel. Furthermore in specific settings where the geometric structure of the support matters, the experimental results show that using a diffusion-based augmentation kernel outperforms the Gaussian one.

Read more

entry.title: Logistic Regression Equivalent Weights for Survey Inference: Construction and Asymptotic Properties

link.title: Logistic Regression Equivalent Weights for Survey Inference: Construction and Asymptotic Properties

entry.content:
Equivalent weights from regression models provide a bridge between design-based and model- based survey inference. We develop a frequentist survey-weighting framework for logistic regres- sion equivalent weights under categorical poststratification. Because the logistic model-based population estimator is nonlinear in the observed outcomes, we define equivalent weights through a local first-order representation, with each weight given by the scaled derivative of the popula- tion estimator with respect to the corresponding observed outcome. This construction yields an explicit closed-form expression in terms of the fitted logistic model and population cell structure. We establish convergence of the effective sample size ratio, asymptotic linearity of the resulting weighted estimator, and a consistent plug-in variance estimator under a finite-cell superpop- ulation framework. Simulation results examine population recovery, regression performance, effective sample size, and the finite-sample behavior of the asymptotic variance approximation. The results show that logistic equivalent weighting provides competitive finite-sample point esti- mation and approximately valid plug-in variance estimation, effective sample size is competitive with alternative model-based weighting in the settings considered. An application to the Fu- ture of Families and Child Wellbeing Study illustrates the construction and use of the proposed weights and variance estimator in an empirical survey setting. We emphasize the relationship between logistic equivalent weighting and recent work on locally equivalent weights for non- linear multilevel regression and poststratification, while focusing specifically on the frequentist interpretation of the weights, their survey-weight properties, and their use for inference.

entry.title: Logistic vegetation trajectories and their implications for land surface phenology

link.title: Logistic vegetation trajectories and their implications for land surface phenology

entry.content:
Vegetation trajectories describe canopy development and underpin phenological metrics, including the start and end of the growing season. We derive a generalized logistic function (GLF) to represent canopy growth under explicit assumptions: exponential development combined with a Michaelis-Menten-type saturating response yields an ordinary logistic function, and a power transformation introduces asymmetry. Using the GLF as a common mathematical basis, we relate trajectory shape to phenological metrics and date uncertainty. We derive shape-dependent relative thresholds for derivative-defined transition points and recover the 9.18% onset threshold for an isolated ordinary logistic growth curve under the small-slope approximation. For a symmetric double-logistic seasonal trajectory, we derive the realized amplitude, full width at half maximum and a critical dimensionless temporal separation between growth and senescence components at which interior third-derivative extrema merge. Exact curvature-change transition points also depend on the metric assigned to the time and response axes. Local noise propagation and 4,800 nonlinear fits show how trajectory geometry affects date uncertainty: additional shape flexibility can reduce bias while increasing uncertainty in the seasonal tails. Together, these results explain how trajectory shape determines the location and existence of phenological transition points and uncertainty in their estimated dates. The framework supports phenology retrieval that preserves the underlying trajectory and interprets each metric through its mathematical definition and uncertainty.

entry.title: Low-order outcomes and clustered designs: combining design and analysis for causal inference under network interference

link.title: Low-order outcomes and clustered designs: combining design and analysis for causal inference under network interference

entry.content:
Variance reduction for causal inference in the presence of network interference is often achieved through either outcome modeling, typically analyzed under unit-randomized Bernoulli designs, or clustered experimental designs, typically analyzed without strong parametric assumptions. In this work, we study the intersection of these two approaches and make the following threefold contributions. First, we present an estimator of the total treatment effect (or global average treatment effect) in low-order outcome models when the data are collected under general experimental designs, generalizing previous results for Bernoulli designs. We refer to this estimator as the pseudoinverse estimator and give bounds on its bias and variance in terms of properties of the experimental design. Second, we evaluate these bounds for the case of Bernoulli graph cluster randomized (GCR) designs. Its variance scales like the smaller of the variance obtained by the estimator derived under a low-order assumption, and the variance obtained from cluster randomization, showing that combining these variance reduction strategies is preferable to using either individually. When the order of the potential outcomes model is correctly specified, our estimator is always unbiased, and under a misspecified model, we upper bound the bias by the closeness of the ground truth model to a low-order model. Third, we give empirical evidence that our variance bounds can be used to select a good clustering that minimizes the worst-case variance under a cluster randomized design from a set of candidate clusterings. Across a range of graphs and clustering algorithms, our method consistently selects clusterings that perform well on a range of response models, suggesting the practical use of our bounds.

entry.title: Manifold Approximation leads to Robust Kernel Alignment

link.title: Manifold Approximation leads to Robust Kernel Alignment

entry.content:
Centered kernel alignment (CKA) is a popular metric for comparing representations, determining equivalence of networks, and conducting neuroscience research. However, CKA does not account for the underlying manifold and relies on numerous heuristics that cause it to behave differently at different scales of data. In this work, we propose Manifold-approximated Kernel Alignment (MKA), which incorporates manifold geometry (i.e., local neighborhood) into the alignment task. We derive a theoretical framework for MKA. Our construction removes representation-dependent degree weighting, yields a closed-form alignment score, and gives each row a probabilistic interpretation as a local Markov transition distribution. We further establish kernel- and score-level stability with respect to the neighborhood size. We perform empirical evaluations on synthetic datasets and real-world examples to characterize and compare MKA to its contemporaries. In controlled synthetic experiments, MKA is consistently less sensitive to hyperparameters and captures the selected topology-preserving relationships. On the large-scale benchmark, MKA achieves its strongest aggregate performance in vision, is competitive on graphs, and is weaker than CKA in several NLP evaluations. Our findings suggest that manifold-aware kernel alignment provides a robust foundation for measuring representations and is potentially useful when local neighborhood geometry is important, with possible applications in representation learning.

entry.title: Margin Certificates for Voting Classifiers under Mixing Dependence

link.title: Margin Certificates for Voting Classifiers under Mixing Dependence

entry.content:
Margin bounds explain why weighted votes generalize after training error vanishes, but dependent observations require concentration arguments that keep the dependence model and failure budget explicit. We study stationary mixing streams without treating dependence as a formal substitution of an “effective sample size.” For a finite base class, we combine independent-block Rademacher theory for stationary $\beta$-mixing processes with a clipped margin loss to obtain an explicit uniform voting-margin certificate, whose dependence penalty is set by the number of approximately independent blocks and the coupling budget $4(\mu-1)\beta(a)$. A black-box transfer theorem shows that any i.i.d. voting-margin guarantee remains valid on a regularly spaced subsequence, with only an additive $\beta$-mixing failure probability. For votes fixed independently of a stationary finite-state reversible Markov stream, spectral concentration gives the cleaner $\sqrt{t_{rel}/n}$ rate, and a sticky-refresh construction shows this exponent is unavoidable. The constant is statistic-specific: the effective sample size is $n/\tau_{int}(g)$, with $\tau_{int}(g) \le 2t_{rel}-1$. When the dependence scale is unknown, a batch-means Student-t interval is valid up to an explicit remainder vanishing in the number of batches, with width governed by $\tau_{int}(g)$ rather than the worst-case $t_{rel}$. Experiments show: the learned-vote certificate is nonvacuous once the block count is large; a two-timescale construction gives a batch-means interval 8.1x narrower than the worst-case interval at nominal coverage (0.945); block-bootstrap and batch-means intervals undercover under strong dependence while the certificate stays valid; and on real, ordered UCI HAR sensor data the dependence-agnostic certificate reaches 0.95 coverage where naive intervals reach only 0.38.

When the dependence scale is unknown, a batch-means Student-t interval is valid up to an explicit remainder vanishing in the number of batches, with width governed by $\tau_{int}(g)$ rather than the worst-case $t_{rel}$. Experiments show: the learned-vote certificate is nonvacuous once the block count is large; a two-timescale construction gives a batch-means interval 8.1x narrower than the worst-case interval at nominal coverage (0.945); block-bootstrap and batch-means intervals undercover under strong dependence while the certificate stays valid; and on real, ordered UCI HAR sensor data the dependence-agnostic certificate reaches 0.95 coverage where naive intervals reach only 0.38.

entry.title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes

link.title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes

entry.content:
Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.

Read more

entry.title: Mediation and moderation in distance-based regression with triangular fuzzy data: simulation evidence and an application to academic performance

link.title: Mediation and moderation in distance-based regression with triangular fuzzy data: simulation evidence and an application to academic performance

entry.content:
We study mediation and moderation in the distance-based regression model for triangular fuzzy responses, in which the center and transformed spreads of the response are linear in the components of fuzzy and crisp covariates. With a common design, componentwise least squares minimizes the unconstrained quadratic extension of the Yang–Ko distance on the transformed scale, for any choice of its shape parameters. Direct, indirect and total effects are defined separately for the center and the spreads of the response as plug-in contrasts on the fitted equations; when the mediator spreads are transformed and carry part of the indirect association, the product-of-coefficients rule no longer holds for the center. Moderation is modeled through triangular interaction regressors and tested with a Freedman–Lane permutation test. In simulations calibrated on real data, percentile bootstrap intervals for the indirect effects had coverage between 0.905 and 0.975, the empirical size of the indirect-effect tests did not exceed 0.085, and ignoring the paths through the mediator spreads biased the indirect effect on the center by 16 to 20\% at every sample size. The fuzzy model predicted better than a centers-only model only from $n=250$. In data on 91 university students collected in 2014, the indirect contrast through a course indicator accounted for about half of the model-based association between prior knowledge and the center of academic performance, the interactions of prior knowledge with sex and with motivation remained after a Holm adjustment, and the spreads of the covariates did not improve leave-one-out prediction.

Read more

entry.title: Mitigating Data Reconstruction Attacks in Federated Learning: Conditions, Bounds, and Theoretical Guarantees

link.title: Mitigating Data Reconstruction Attacks in Federated Learning: Conditions, Bounds, and Theoretical Guarantees

entry.content:
Privacy attacks, particularly data reconstruction attacks, pose significant challenges to federated learning despite its promise in privacy-preserving collaborative training. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of privacy leakage in federated learning through dual perspectives: linear algebra and optimization theory. By analyzing the client-update Jacobian, we identify conditions under which distinct data batches produce the same model update and derive a sufficient batch-size criterion for non-unique reconstruction. Through optimization theory, we establish a novel upper bound for privacy leakage that incorporates batch size, distortion extent, and other critical parameters. These theoretical insights elucidate the fundamental relationships between system parameters and privacy vulnerability, laying the groundwork for developing more robust privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks.

Read more

entry.title: Modeling Ordinal Survey Data with Unfolding Models

link.title: Modeling Ordinal Survey Data with Unfolding Models

entry.content:
Surveys that rely on ordinal polychotomous (Likert-like) items are widely employed to capture individual preferences because they allow respondents to express both the direction and strength of their preferences. Latent factor models traditionally used in this context implicitly assume that the response functions (the cumulative distribution of the ordinal outcome) are monotonic on the latent trait. This assumption can be too restrictive in several application areas, including in political science and marketing. In this work, we propose a novel ordinal probit unfolding model that can accommodate both monotonic and non-monotonic response functions. The advantages of the model are illustrated by analyzing an immigration attitude survey conducted in the United States.

Read more

entry.title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention

link.title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention

entry.content:
A universal forecaster is trained once and applied everywhere, so it must serve tasks whose schemas, forecast horizons, and temporal resolutions all differ. The number of targets and covariates changes from dataset to dataset, horizons vary by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates range from seconds to years. Existing time-series foundation models address these only in part, since they isolate each series or visit the two grid relations in separate blocks, and they fix the horizon and resolution before training begins. We introduce Morpheus-2.0, a compact encoder-only foundation model that represents targets and covariates on a single variable-time grid. Its dual-axis attention runs both relations side by side in every layer, one across variables at a timestep and one across time within a variable; a learned gate weights the two per layer, and an axis-aware rotary encoding preserves both grid coordinates. The forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights spans short to long horizons at no additional inference cost. Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale extends the model to several temporal resolutions at once, weighting them according to the series being forecast. Across GIFT-Eval, which spans several domains and frequencies, the two models give complementary operating points: Morpheus-2.0 attains 0.685 relative MASE with 81M parameters, while the larger Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale attains 0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the lowest of any published system on both metrics.

Read more

entry.title: Multi-Resolution Analysis of Variable Selection for Road Safety in St. Louis and Its Neighboring Area

link.title: Multi-Resolution Analysis of Variable Selection for Road Safety in St. Louis and Its Neighboring Area

entry.content:
Generally, Lasso, Adaptive Lasso, and SCAD are standard approaches in variable selection in the presence of a large number of predictors. In recent years, during intensity function estimation for spatial point processes with a diverging number of predictors, many researchers have considered these penalized methods. But we have discussed a multi-resolution perspective for the variable selection method for spatial point process data. Its advantage is twofold: it not only efficiently selects the predictors but also provides the idea of which points are liable for selecting a predictor at a specific resolution. Actually, our research is motivated by the crime and accident occurrences in St. Louis and its neighborhoods. It is more relevant to select predictors at the local level, and thus we get the idea of which set of predictors is relevant for the occurrences of crime or accident in which parts of St. Louis. We describe the simulation results to justify the accuracy of local-level variable selection during intensity function estimation.

Read more

entry.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach

link.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach

entry.content:
High throughput sequencing technology is routinely used to generate high dimensional (HD) count data. One objective is to determine which variables are associated with a covariate via the testing of multiple null hypotheses, say $H_m:\beta_m = 0$ for $m = 1, 2, …, M$ where each $\beta_m$ is a regression parameter. The standard approach computes a $p$-value for each null hypothesis and applies some false discovery rate (FDR) method to determine which null hypotheses are rejected, i.e. which variables can be discovered as associated with the covariate. However, even if data are well modeled'', this approach tends to provide a misleading list of discoveries in that someuninteresting’’ negligible associations ($\beta_m \approx 0$) are discovered, while other interesting associations are not. This paper formally addresses this issue using Poisson Mixture models and a Local FDR (PMLFDR) procedure for testing of multiple composite null hypotheses $H_m:\beta_m\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$. It is shown that PMLFDR procedures allow for consistently estimable expressions for overdispersion, provide asymptotically optimal FDR control, and are robust with respect to model misspecification. Simulation studies and real data analysis illustrate that PMLFDR procedures perform favorably compared to established procedures in that they a) are flexible enough to model most HD count data regardless of the technology used in generation b) allow for continuous and categorical covariates and c) yield more meaningful discoveries without sacrificing FDR control.

Read more

entry.title: Multivariate M-extremiles

link.title: Multivariate M-extremiles

entry.content:
Extremiles represent an important class of distributional functionals defined through weighted squared loss functions, providing a valuable alternative to quantiles and expectiles. To date, their development has remained confined to the univariate setting. Here we introduce a robust multivariate extension of extremiles for random vectors by combining a directional weighting mechanism with Huber’s multidimensional loss function. The proposed definition yields a family of directional extremiles indexed by a tuning parameter controlling the degree of robustness to outliers, with the quadratic-loss geometric extremile arising as a limiting case. We prove their main theoretical properties and introduce the notion of extremile sets. From an inferential perspective, we develop an efficient two-step procedure based on iteratively reweighted least squares, and derive asymptotic properties using the theory of Z-estimators. The finite-sample behavior of the proposed methodology is investigated through simulation experiments under Gaussian, contaminated, and heavy-tailed settings. An application to daily returns of three major cryptocurrencies illustrates its practical utility on financial data.

Read more

entry.title: Muon Dynamics as a Spectral Wasserstein Flow

link.title: Muon Dynamics as a Spectral Wasserstein Flow

entry.content:
Gradient normalization can stabilize deep-learning optimization, and spectral normalizations are especially natural for matrix-shaped parameter blocks; Muon is the motivating example. We study an idealized deterministic, continuous-time, vanishing-momentum version of this idea in the mean-field regime, where wide models are represented by probability measures on parameter space. Starting from normalized matrix flows, we introduce Spectral Wasserstein distances indexed by norms $\gamma$ on positive semidefinite matrices: the trace norm recovers the classical $W_2$ distance, the operator norm gives the Muon geometry, and Schatten norms interpolate between them. We develop a static Kantorovich formulation, a max–min robust-cost representation, and Gaussian reductions extending the Bures formula. For monotone norms, we prove equivalence with a Benamou–Brenier formulation and obtain a gradient-flow interpretation of normalized mean-field training dynamics. Numerical experiments illustrate the resulting flows for MMD objectives, Gaussian reductions, two-layer ReLU models, and shallow attention.

Read more

entry.title: Mutual Information Constrained Chernoff Bottleneck

link.title: Mutual Information Constrained Chernoff Bottleneck

entry.content:
The classical information bottleneck (IB) measures the relevance of a representation $U$ of $X$ to a target $Y$ by $I(U;Y)$, which does not directly characterize the error of downstream decisions. For a binary hypothesis $Y$ inferred from many separately encoded observations, the optimal error exponent is the Chernoff information between the two conditional distributions of $U$ given $Y$. We study the mutual information constrained Chernoff bottleneck, which seeks an encoder that maximizes this Chernoff information subject to a rate constraint $I(U;X) \leq R$. We show that its optimal value $C(R)$ increases strictly up to $R = H(V)$, where $V$ merges the symbols of $X$ with equal likelihood ratio, remains at the uncompressed exponent beyond, and, unlike the IB curve, need not be concave. We further show that $k+1$ outputs suffice to attain $C(R)$, where $k$ is the cardinality of $V$. We propose an alternating algorithm that updates the encoder via a generalized Blahut–Arimoto algorithm and the Chernoff parameter $s$ via a nonlinear equation, and prove that its iterates remain feasible, with nondecreasing and convergent Chernoff information. Comparing with the classical IB for $n$ samples, we show that, whenever the two objectives disagree, the IB encoder has the smaller equivocation $H(Y U^{n})$ at $n = 1$, whereas the Chernoff bottleneck has the smaller error probability and equivocation for all large $n$. Numerical experiments confirm the theory, and on real topic-detection data from the 20 Newsgroups corpus, compressing each word to only $17\%$ of its entropy retains $90\%$ of the error exponent and nearly the accuracy of the uncompressed classifier.

Read more

entry.title: Nash Equilibrium Individualized Treatment Regimes under Network Interference

link.title: Nash Equilibrium Individualized Treatment Regimes under Network Interference

entry.content:
Network interference creates a fundamental tension in optimal individualized treatment regime learning: maximizing overall population outcomes may come at the expense of some individuals’ outcomes. Existing optimal individualized treatment regime methods under interference primarily target population-level objectives without accounting for individual optimality. Motivated by this tension, we introduce Nash equilibrium individualized treatment regimes, or simply Nash regimes, which directly target individual optimality under interference. Under a Nash regime, no individual can improve their conditional expected outcome through unilateral deviation when all other individuals follow the regime. We establish conditions for the existence of Nash regimes. When no exact Nash regime exists, we introduce an $\alpha^*$-Nash regime as an alternative target that minimizes regret relative to individual optimality. We then develop Nash learning, a doubly robust procedure for estimating the proposed regimes. Under a super-population random-graph framework accommodating both sparse and dense networks, we characterize how network sparsity and treatment assignment mechanisms affect estimation performance. Simulations and a real-data application demonstrate that Nash learning improves individual optimality while maintaining competitive population-level performance.

Read more

entry.title: Native Probability Outputs for Clinical Triage: An Evaluation of Calibration and Decision Accuracy

link.title: Native Probability Outputs for Clinical Triage: An Evaluation of Calibration and Decision Accuracy

entry.content:
Patient-facing triage requires an appropriate care recommendation and recognition of when information is insufficient. We evaluate whether Jev, a decision model that returns probabilities over predefined actions, supports both judgments. Using CARE-Bench, we compare Jev with four general-purpose language models and three input-independent baselines across 925 decision points from 439 public cases. On the public test subset, Jev ranks fourth of five models by macro-F1 (0.461) but has the lowest observed multiclass Brier score (0.610), an 18.7\% improvement over uniform prediction (case-bootstrap 95\% interval, 4.9–31.1\%). Noul has lower binary Brier than Choice (0.215 versus 0.276). A evaluation of 453 HealthBench conversations again gives Jev the lowest observed Brier score (0.299), but measures a distinct emergency-referral judgment. Jev combines lower probability error with missed clarification needs in the four-action task. Asking about information sufficiency separately increases recall but also produces frequent unnecessary clarification assignments.

Read more

entry.title: Nesting or resolution? Facility proxies for variance estimation versus confounding adjustment in claims data without facility identifiers

link.title: Nesting or resolution? Facility proxies for variance estimation versus confounding adjustment in claims data without facility identifiers

entry.content:
In claims databases, facility identifiers are often removed during de-identification, leaving only coarse attributes such as bed size. Yet facility information is needed for variance estimation, confounding adjustment and assessment of treatment availability. We examined whether accreditation-gated billing items can build strata standing for hospitals, and how to construct a facility proxy for each use. In 1,730,736 adults undergoing surgery (Medical Data Vision database, Japan, 2019-2023), we built marker-pattern strata from 66 accreditation-gated receipt codes (markers) and evaluated each grouping against a true facility identifier in an insurer-based database (DeSC Healthcare) and in simulation. The variance explained by the marker-pattern strata decreased with the extent to which a variable was patient- rather than hospital-determined ($R^2$ 0.921 for an accreditation item, 0.036 for sex). For variance estimation, the supplied-attribute cells, which can merge but never split hospitals, kept the type I error rate at 4.8% with a wild cluster bootstrap, against 5.4% for the true identifier and 39% when clustering was ignored; every finer marker-based grouping did worse. For adjustment, evaluated with real facility-level confounders and simulated null exposures, the marker pattern removed 51% of the confounding related to accreditation-linked facility characteristics, against 8% for the cells. The proportion of patients in groups mixing hospitals with and without the relevant accreditation was 49% for the marker pattern against 98% for the cells. No single facility proxy serves every purpose: nesting governs variance estimation, and resolution governs adjustment and treatment availability. Without a facility identifier, the supplied-attribute cells can carry the standard errors, and marker-pattern strata are worth considering for the other two uses.

entry.title: On Reparameterizing the Score Function

link.title: On Reparameterizing the Score Function

entry.content:
Policy gradients for autoregressive sequence models differentiate each token’s log-probability while holding the conditioning history fixed. This discards information about how earlier decisions shape later conditional distributions, creating a credit-assignment bottleneck when rewards are sparse. We introduce History-Reparameterized (HR) policy gradients, which replace the frozen prefix in the score function with a differentiable reparameterized or relaxed history, allowing gradients of downstream log-probabilities to propagate backward through the generated trajectory. The resulting history-pathwise term is generally biased when added directly, so we derive Optimal HR (OHR), a centered control-variate estimator with a closed-form coefficient that minimizes the trace of the gradient variance at the population level. The variance reduction is governed by temporal structure in the policy dynamics: random or weakly structured policies provide little benefit, while policies with learned sequential dependencies yield informative history-pathwise corrections. For discrete tokens, the choice of relaxation is crucial: embedding-level relaxation yields substantial variance reduction that grows with horizon, whereas straight-through Gumbel-Softmax yields essentially none in our diagnostics. We validate the method on a Gaussian linear Markov model, a sparse-reward T-maze with a recurrent policy, and an autoregressive Transformer model for small Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) instances.

entry.title: Online detection of distributional changes for time series in metric spaces

link.title: Online detection of distributional changes for time series in metric spaces

entry.content:
We propose an online testing framework for detecting distributional changes in serially dependent data with values in a separable metric space. Based on two-sample $U$-statistics, the framework encompasses sequential analogs of energy distance and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) procedures while accommodating temporal dependence. We establish asymptotic theory for finite and open-ended monitoring horizons that characterizes the full asymptotic run-length distribution under $H_0$ and yields asymptotic false-alarm control. We further establish new spectral approximation results for kernel matrices formed from serially dependent observations, and use them to construct a feasible Monte Carlo calibration procedure. Our flexible window construction encompasses classical, Page-type, and full-scan historical-baseline monitoring and can achieve short detection delays for both early and late changepoints, without requiring sub-Gaussianity or high-order moments of the raw observations. Simulations show reliable false-alarm control across linear, nonlinear, high-dimensional, and functional time-series models and further demonstrate that, over a broad range of alternatives and changepoint locations, the proposed method can achieve substantially shorter delays than recent procedures designed specifically for rapid detection. Applications to foreign exchange rates, electricity-market curves, and daily air transportation networks illustrate the methodology across scalar, functional, and network-valued time series.

entry.title: On the Role of Batch Size in Stochastic Conditional Gradient Methods

link.title: On the Role of Batch Size in Stochastic Conditional Gradient Methods

entry.content:
We study the role of batch size in stochastic conditional gradient methods under a $\mu$-Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz ($\mu$-KL) condition. Focusing on momentum-based stochastic conditional gradient algorithms (e.g., Scion), we derive a new analysis that explicitly captures the interaction between stepsize, batch size, and stochastic noise. Our study reveals a regime-dependent behavior: increasing the batch size initially improves optimization accuracy but, beyond a critical threshold, the benefits saturate and can eventually degrade performance under a fixed token budget. Notably, the theory predicts the magnitude of the optimal stepsize and aligns well with empirical practices observed in large-scale training. Leveraging these insights, we derive principled guidelines for selecting the batch size and stepsize, and propose an adaptive strategy that increases batch size and sequence length during training while preserving convergence guarantees. Experiments on NanoGPT are consistent with the theoretical predictions and illustrate the emergence of the predicted scaling regimes. Overall, our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding batch size scaling in stochastic conditional gradient methods and offer guidance for designing efficient training schedules in large-scale optimization.

Read more

entry.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing

link.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing

entry.content:
Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding (BIHT) is a simple, yet effective, greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from one-bit sign measurements. In its original form, BIHT performs a ``gradient-descent’’ step, followed by hard thresholding. A convergence analysis of this algorithm was left open in the introductory work of Jacques, Laska, Boufounos, and Baraniuk [IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory (2013)] and has remained unresolved for over a decade, with subsequent sharp analyses studying a {\em normalized variant} instead, that additionally projects every iterate onto the unit sphere. This paper resolves that gap and characterizes when per-iteration normalization is algorithmically necessary. In the noiseless setting, we prove a universal, sample-optimal convergence theorem for the original BIHT algorithm. Specifically, with $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ measurements, a deterministic, computable finite-time iterate has directional error at most $\epsilon$, simultaneously for every $s$-sparse unit vector. This matches the optimal sample dependence achieved by normalized BIHT in prior work. Under sign corruptions, we prove a sharp separation. If at most a $\tau$ fraction of signs are flipped adversarially, then BIHT, without per-iterate normalization, still reaches the robust error floor at an early iterate with a matching $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ sample complexity rate as its normalized variant. This recovery, however, is not stable. We prove a scalar lower bound showing that any nontrivial corruption pattern, even one that involves only one flipped sign together with one clean sign, forces the iterates to oscillate indefinitely. Consequently, no general last-iterate convergence theorem can hold for BIHT under sign corruptions, while its normalized surrogate provably escapes this instance.

Read more

entry.title: On the analysis of sequential designs without a specified number of observations

link.title: On the analysis of sequential designs without a specified number of observations

entry.content:
The paper focuses on sequential experiments whose outcomes, success or failure, can be expressed using a binomial distribution, and in which whether or not a further experiment is made depends on the prior outcomes. Examples include subsequent medical interventions until a target response is achieved. The maximum likelihood estimate of the treatment success probability is the ratio of the number of observed successes and the total number of times the treatment was administered. Despite a prespecified initial sample size, the total number of conducted interventions cannot be determined in advance, and the estimated total number of successes may not be equal to the one observed, so the estimated variance of success probability is not that of a binomial distribution. These results generalize to designs with a tree structure consisting of groups of the experiments with group-specific outcome distributions. The multiplicative models entailed are studied using the tools from algebraic statistics and the theory of relational models. The estimates of success probabilities and their covariance are derived and shown to depend on the structural properties of the relevant exponential family.

entry.title: Optimal Cox regression under federated differential privacy: coefficients and cumulative hazards

link.title: Optimal Cox regression under federated differential privacy: coefficients and cumulative hazards

entry.content:
We study two canonical problems in distributed survival analysis under federated differential privacy (FDP): estimation of cumulative hazard functions and Cox regression coefficients, allowing for heterogeneous per-server sample sizes and privacy budgets. To quantify the fundamental cost of privacy, we derive minimax lower and upper bounds that match up to poly-logarithmic factors, revealing server-level phase transitions between private and non-private regimes. Our algorithms are computationally-efficient and are based on adapting differentially private binary tree and gradient descent algorithms to handle estimating equations with dependent terms. We also study three related problems: estimation of the cumulative baseline hazard and survival functions in the Cox model under FDP, and estimation of regression coefficients under the federated label differential privacy, a relaxed privacy notion. For these problems, we develop efficient algorithms, establish theoretical guarantees and investigate minimax optimality. Numerical experiments, including a real-data application, support the theoretical findings. The proposed methods are implemented in the accompanying R package FDPCox.

Read more

entry.title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Efficiency Characterization

link.title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Efficiency Characterization

entry.content:
Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach uses an $F$-weighted portfolio with a predefined prior $F$. For suitable priors, this approach has recently been shown to achieve the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, the prior $F$ changes how the portfolio test behaves near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and introduce an efficiency measure that allows the error probability and alternative to vary jointly. Under mild assumptions, we prove that efficiency equals a logarithmic decay index of the prior near zero. This gives a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality: Beta priors have infinite efficiency, whereas suitable Robbins-type priors attain efficiency 1. As an application, we consider testing a specified mean of a bounded random variable and describe an implementation of the portfolio algorithm with almost-linear computational complexity.

Read more

entry.title: Optimal product launch in uncertain competitive markets: A multi-agent adversarial risk analysis framework

link.title: Optimal product launch in uncertain competitive markets: A multi-agent adversarial risk analysis framework

entry.content:
Product launching is a nuanced problem that entails choosing numerous decision variables, including timing, pricing, quality, and marketing strategy. Furthermore, decision-makers must account for multiple uncertainty sources. These include endogenous factors, such as product quality and the strategic decisions of competitors and consumers; as well as exogenous elements, like market evolution and regulations. This paper proposes a novel general framework to support product launch decisions in the presence of multiple competitors and buyers using adversarial risk analysis, mitigating the strong common-knowledge assumptions typical of standard game-theoretic approaches in this domain. We also introduce variants that account for multiple product purchases and integrate discrete choice models. To overcome the inherent computational intractability of modeling multi-agent strategic uncertainty, we deploy a simulation-optimization approach leveraging Bayesian optimization. Finally, we illustrate our proposed framework through a software launch case study focused on optimal timing, pricing, and quality decisions.

Read more

entry.title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments

link.title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments

entry.content:
Regulatory approval of products in high-stakes domains such as drug development requires statistical evidence of safety and efficacy through large-scale randomized controlled trials. However, the high financial cost of these trials may deter developers who lack absolute certainty in their product’s efficacy, ultimately stifling the development of `moonshot’ products that could offer high social utility. To address this inefficiency, in this paper, we introduce a statistical protocol for experimentation where the product developer (the agent) conducts a randomized controlled trial sequentially and the regulator (the principal) partially subsidizes its cost. By modeling the protocol using a belief Markov decision process, we show that the agent’s optimal strategy can be found efficiently using dynamic programming. Further, we show that the social utility is a piecewise linear and convex function over the subsidy level the principal selects, and thus the socially optimal subsidy can also be found efficiently using divide-and-conquer. Simulation experiments using publicly available data on antibiotic development and approval demonstrate that our statistical protocol can be used to increase social utility by more than $35$$\%$ relative to standard, non-sequential protocols.

Read more

entry.title: PICKLES: Covariance-Preconditioned Kinetic Langevin Ensemble Sampler

link.title: PICKLES: Covariance-Preconditioned Kinetic Langevin Ensemble Sampler

entry.content:
We propose a covariance-preconditioned kinetic Langevin ensemble sampler named PICKLES. This is a kinetic analogue of the affine invariant interacting Langevin dynamics (ALDI). PICKLES uses a rectangular covariance square root as a preconditioner to avoid computing matrix inverses or square roots, leading to position and momentum variables of different dimensions. Theoretically, the continuous-time dynamics are ergodic under mild regularity and growth conditions on the potential, assuming $N>d+1$ particles and a full-rank initial ensemble. We discretize PICKLES using BAOAB or OBABO splitting, with the latter convenient for Metropolization. For Gaussian targets at stationarity, we demonstrate that Metropolized PICKLES achieves an integration step size scaling of $d^{-1/4}$ to achieve fixed acceptance probabilities, as the ensemble size and dimension increase at a fixed ratio. This matches the scaling of single particle Metropolized Hamiltonian and kinetic samplers. Numerical experiments compare sampling efficiency and estimation error with non-preconditioned, overdamped, and single-chain counterparts, demonstrating improved efficiency per gradient evaluation. On a Dark Energy Survey Year 1 3x2pt cosmology benchmark, we obtain competitive effective sample size per gradient evaluation compared to a densely preconditioned No-U-Turn Sampler.

Read more

entry.title: PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors

link.title: PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors

entry.content:
Clustered and personalised federated learning (FL) needs a signal telling the server which clients should share a model. Most methods derive it from losses or model updates that must be recomputed during training. We study pTopoFL, which derives it once, before training, from a compact persistent-homology (PH) descriptor of each client’s feature distribution: the server clusters clients on these descriptors, weights them within clusters, and runs blended clustered local gradient descent, returning one personalised model per cluster. For strongly convex, smooth losses we analyse the complete procedure: for any partition, one round is a contraction with factor (1-eta*mu)^tau; the fixed point is characterised by a local-step drift bound, an exact formula for the effective strength of blending (which yields a calibration rule) and a stochastic floor exposing a bias-variance trade-off of clustering; and personalisation lowers the heterogeneity floor in proportion to a measurable share of the dispersion of client optima. Experiments on synthetic federations, a label-skew benchmark and a real four-hospital dataset confirm the theory and delimit the method. When feature geometry and decision rules co-vary, the PH partition recovers the latent client groups, including differences a linear-subspace descriptor misses, and pTopoFL is competitive with the strongest clustered baselines; on the real federation it lowers the test log-loss of FedAvg from 0.463 to 0.438, on par with the best personalised methods. When heterogeneity is invisible in feature geometry, it offers no advantage over FedAvg. pTopoFL transmits model parameters and is no more private than FedAvg; we give a record-level differential-privacy accounting and show that privatising the descriptor destroys the partition. Code reproduces every number.

entry.title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials

link.title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials

entry.content:
Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material’s internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.

Read more

entry.title: Post-Selection Distributional Model Evaluation

link.title: Post-Selection Distributional Model Evaluation

entry.content:
Formal model evaluation methods typically certify that a model satisfies a prescribed target key performance indicator (KPI) level. However, in many applications, the relevant target KPI level may not be known a priori, and the user may instead wish to compare candidate models by analyzing the full trade-offs between performance and reliability achievable at test time by the models. This task, requiring the reliable estimate of the test-time KPI distributions, is made more complicated by the fact that the same data must often be used both to pre-select a subset of candidate models and to estimate their KPI distributions, causing a potential post-selection bias. In this work, we introduce post-selection distributional model evaluation (PS-DME), a general framework for statistically valid distributional model assessment after arbitrary data-dependent model pre-selection. Building on e-values, PS-DME controls post-selection false coverage rate (FCR) for the distributional KPI estimates and we establish explicit conditions under which it is provably more sample efficient than a baseline method based on sample splitting. Experiments on synthetic data, text-to-SQL decoding with large language models, and telecom network performance evaluation demonstrate that PS-DME enables reliable comparison of candidate configurations across a range of reliability levels, supporting the statistically reliable exploration of performance–reliability trade-offs.

Read more

entry.title: Prior-Amortized In-Context Bayesian Inference for Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models

link.title: Prior-Amortized In-Context Bayesian Inference for Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models

entry.content:
Hierarchical data is ubiquitous in the empirical sciences and most commonly analyzed with generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs), which have interpretable parameters. Bayesian inference for GLMMs yields calibrated uncertainty estimates but requires Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC); the gold-standard No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) is slow and must restart for every new dataset, model and prior specification. We introduce MetaBeta, a pretrained amortized model for in-context Bayesian inference over GLMMs. The full prior and model specification are supplied as context at test time, and the model returns an asymptotically exact posterior at the speed of a forward pass. Two set transformers and two conditional neural spline flows mirror the GLMM’s hierarchical structure and are trained jointly on millions of realistic simulated datasets with continuous, binary and count outcomes. The flow posterior is refined by Independence Metropolis-Hastings against the unnormalized posterior, yielding tuning-free asymptotically correct inference. Alternatively, MetaBeta warm-starts NUTS, yielding nearly identical inference 3.5-13x faster than its cold-started counterpart, while removing over 98% of its divergent transitions. On controlled benchmarks with ground-truth parameters, MetaBeta matches NUTS in parameter recovery, posterior calibration and out-of-sample prediction; on real datasets with unknown parameters, priors and model structure, its posteriors closely agree with those of NUTS; and it remains faithful where amortized models typically struggle: under misspecified likelihoods, misspecified priors, out-of-distribution predictors, collinear designs and data-poor regimes. On real data, a full prior sensitivity analysis including model comparison takes a few seconds with MetaBeta against 14-18 core-hours for NUTS, tracing its posteriors throughout. Our model is open-source and open-weights.

entry.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions

link.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions

entry.content:
We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$—whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded—the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO). Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator’s output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors. Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead. Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.

entry.title: Quantifying Uncertainty Bounds in Spectral Shallow Water Bathymetry: The Profile Likelihood Framework for Semi-Analytical Models

link.title: Quantifying Uncertainty Bounds in Spectral Shallow Water Bathymetry: The Profile Likelihood Framework for Semi-Analytical Models

entry.content:
Accurate bathymetric mapping in shallow waters is critical for coastal monitoring, navigation safety, and environmental conservation. While semi-analytical (SA) models have proven effective for estimating water column depth (WCD) from optical remote sensing data, quantifying the associated uncertainties remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a unified framework based on profile likelihood to evaluate WCD uncertainties in Semi-Analytical (SA) models, bridging traditional variance-covariance methods with likelihood-based inference. Through controlled simulations, we systematically assess the performance of first-order statistical tests-likelihood ratio, Wald (observed and expected), and score tests-across varying environmental conditions and sensor configurations.<p>Our results demonstrate that the expected Fisher information Wald test, equivalent to classical variance-covariance propagation, provides reliable uncertainty bounds in hyperspectral settings with clear waters. However, its performance deteriorates in multispectral applications and complex water conditions, where likelihood ratio tests prove more robust. This divergence highlights fundamental limitations in the small-sample regime typical of per-pixel spectral bathymetry. Notably, even under idealized conditions with true parameter initialization, local optimization challenges in SA models can compromise both parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, suggesting even greater challenges in practical applications with less favorable initialization. The findings underscore the importance of robust statistical inference in improving the reliability of bathymetric products for operational applications.</p>

entry.title: R2-GP: Variance-Calibrated Priors for Additive Gaussian Processes

link.title: R2-GP: Variance-Calibrated Priors for Additive Gaussian Processes

entry.content:
We develop R2-GP, an R2D2-type prior for Gaussian process (GP) generalised additive models (GAMs) that calibrates explained variance ($R^2$) for Mat'ern covariance kernels. The function variance for standard Mat'ern kernels depends jointly on the effect magnitude and length-scale. As such, smooth and rough components with identical amplitudes contribute very different amounts of variation. With independent priors on component amplitudes, this variation results in variance overestimation, especially in higher dimensions. We overcome this by taking direct control over each component’s expected contribution to prior explained variance. We do this by rescaling each component based on its length scale and observed inputs, and modelling each rescaled variance as a share of the function variance induced by a global $R^2$ prior. This allows R2-GP to scale well to many components. To also scale to large sample sizes, we extend R2-GP to Hilbert space approximation methods, a framework for kernels exploiting their spectral decompositions for fast and efficient inference. Our simulations and real-world case studies demonstrate superior generalisation and parameter recovery over independent variance priors.

Read more

entry.title: RLTLDR: Self-improvement by Internalizing Self-generated Feedback

link.title: RLTLDR: Self-improvement by Internalizing Self-generated Feedback

entry.content:
The common paradigm of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is to let agents make multiple attempts at a task, and optimize towards the successful ones. This becomes problematic in the realms of self-improvement, where tasks are so difficult that the agent has a low or even no chance of success, and where there are no teacher models or example solutions to distill from. In this paper, we introduce RLTLDR. After each failed attempt, we show the policy the verifier outputs and let it write its own feedback, in the form of a single TL;DR insight. The next rollout is conditioned on all previous insights, and we sequentially sample rollouts until a solution is found. Moreover, we enable backpropagation on the in-context insights to internalize a direct task to insight mapping. On challenging tool-calling and coding datasets (filtered to Pass@128=0), standard GRPO training of a Qwen 3.5 9B Thinking policy stays flat at a Pass@1 of 0% to 1%. RLTLDR breaks through this learning barrier, achieving a Pass@1 of 14-31% with insights in context during training and, crucially, 12-13% when no insight is in context at eval time. We identify that the key is the task to insight internalization. To study this further, we reduce our approach to SFTLDR, training only on (task, insight) tuples, without showing or backpropagating on any rollouts. Training on only 4k of these tuples recovers almost the full performance of RLTLDR and classical SFT on full rollouts. This demonstrates a promising compacted training paradigm of the form “on this sort of task, keep this sort of thing in mind”, which we hope to inspire future research on.

Read more

entry.title: Recurrent Self-Attention Dynamics: An Energy-Agnostic Perspective from Jacobians

link.title: Recurrent Self-Attention Dynamics: An Energy-Agnostic Perspective from Jacobians

entry.content:
The theoretical understanding of self-attention (SA) has been steadily progressing. A prominent line of work studies a class of SA layers that admit an energy function decreased by state updates. While it provides valuable insights into inherent biases in signal propagation, it often relies on idealized assumptions or additional constraints not necessarily present in standard SA. Thus, to broaden our understanding, this work aims to relax these energy constraints and provide an energy-agnostic characterization of inference dynamics by dynamical systems analysis. In more detail, we first consider relaxing the symmetry and single-head constraints traditionally required in energy-based formulations. Next, we show that analyzing the Jacobian matrix of the state is highly valuable when investigating more general SA architectures without necessarily admitting an energy function. It reveals that the normalization layer plays an essential role in suppressing the Lipschitzness of SA and the Jacobian’s complex eigenvalues, which correspond to the oscillatory components of the dynamics. In addition, the Lyapunov exponents computed from the Jacobians demonstrate that the normalized dynamics lie close to a critical state, and this criticality serves as a strong indicator of high inference performance. Furthermore, the Jacobian perspective also enables us to develop regularization methods for training and a pseudo-energy for monitoring inference dynamics.

Read more

entry.title: Regional summaries of Bayesian model uncertainty

link.title: Regional summaries of Bayesian model uncertainty

entry.content:
Bayesian posterior uncertainty can be spread across many models that share the same substantive pattern. Lists of individual models can obscure this structure, while marginal summaries do not describe which configurations are jointly supported. We study how to represent joint model uncertainty through a compact collection of interpretable regions, each grouping models that share a specified pattern. We formulate this task as minimizing representation complexity subject to retaining a prescribed posterior mass within an analyst-supplied family. To address unknown regional probabilities, we develop Adaptive Regional Selection (ARS), which combines adaptive exploration and regional weight estimation with conservative and optimistic selection. These complementary problems identify a summary meeting the mass target and bound how much further its complexity could improve. Under valid regional bounds, we establish guarantees for retained mass, total-variation error, and suboptimality, together with conditions for certifying optimality. We also show that, under bounded within-region weight variation, sufficient sample counts for regional estimation need not grow with the number of represented models, and construct bounds that remain valid under adaptive sampling and stopping. Empirical studies illustrate regional summaries in Bayesian model averaging and Bayesian networks, examining retained mass, representation complexity, and certification.

Read more

entry.title: Reinforcement Learning for Individual Optimal Policy from Heterogeneous Data

link.title: Reinforcement Learning for Individual Optimal Policy from Heterogeneous Data

entry.content:
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to find optimal policies in dynamic environments in order to maximize the expected total rewards by leveraging pre-collected data. Learning from heterogeneous data is one of the fundamental challenges in offline RL. Traditional methods focus on learning an optimal policy for all individuals with pre-collected data from a single episode or homogeneous batch episodes, and thus, may result in a suboptimal policy for a heterogeneous population. In this paper, we propose an individualized offline policy optimization framework for heterogeneous time-stationary Markov decision processes (MDPs). The proposed heterogeneous model with individual latent variables enables us to efficiently estimate the individual Q-functions, and our Penalized Pessimistic Personalized Policy Learning (P4L) algorithm guarantees a fast rate on the average regret under a weak partial coverage assumption on behavior policies. In addition, our simulation studies and a real data application demonstrate the superior numerical performance of the proposed method compared with existing methods.

Read more

entry.title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies

link.title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies

entry.content:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly proposed as a fast solver for unit commitment (UC), but standalone agents remain far more expensive than mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). In the first study of RL on the 51-generator, 72-hour benchmark of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition, we trace this gap to the agents’ own exploration, close most of it, and show that the resulting policy can accelerate an exact solver. In every configuration tested, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and an action-branching Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained from scratch committed about twice the units of a thermal-only MILP optimum, at 39-64% higher cost, whereas a merit-order rule came within 1.6-7% (10-24% when unserved energy is priced). When each unit’s decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random de-commitments. Consistent with this, injecting exploration noise during fine-tuning enlarged a lean policy’s fleet, a reward without shaping terms did not remove the over-commitment, and under their training noise the agents outperformed the rule subjected to comparable noise. Imitating the MILP solutions and fine-tuning conservatively brought PPO within 2.6% of the optimum, and these policies had the lowest penalised cost of any evaluated (about 5%). Fixing the fine-tuned policy’s confident decisions made the MILP 3.8-8.5 times faster within 0.10-0.25% of the best solution, with a smaller worst case than an imitation-only policy fixing as many variables (1.1% against 8.9%). Because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift the reported optimality ratio by up to 3.6% and 9%, we propose a reporting protocol.

entry.title: Relative Jump Distance: a diagnostic for Nested Sampling

link.title: Relative Jump Distance: a diagnostic for Nested Sampling

entry.content:
Nested sampling is widely used in astrophysics and cosmology to reliably infer model parameters and compare models within a Bayesian framework. To address models with many parameters, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) random walks are used within nested sampling to advance a live point population. Diagnostics for nested sampling inference are essential to verify that trustworthy astrophysical conclusions can be drawn. We develop a diagnostic to identify poorly mixed random walks that do not meet the requirements of nested sampling. The distance from the start to the end of the random walk, the jump distance, is compared to the typical neighbour distance between live points, to obtain a relative jump distance (RJD). A robust estimate of a typical neighbour Mahalanobis distance is obtained with the MLFriends algorithm. In mock and real-world inference applications such as inferring the distance to GW170817, we observe the relative jump distance. We propose the geometric mean and fraction of RJD>1 as new summary diagnostics. To evaluate the sensitivity of the new diagnostics, problematic runs are identified by comparison with reruns using much longer MCMC chains. Trustworthy inference runs are consistently associated with above 1.1, while problematic runs can fall below these thresholds. The RJD is more sensitive than previous tests based on the live point insertion order. The RJD diagnostic is proposed as a widely applicable diagnostic to verify inference with nested sampling. It is implemented in the UltraNest package in version 4.1.

Read more

entry.title: Relaxation times of non-reversible Markov processes

link.title: Relaxation times of non-reversible Markov processes

entry.content:
We develop a systematic approach to quantify $L^2$-relaxation times for non-reversible Markov processes based on the singular value gap of the generator introduced by Chatterjee. The inverse of the singular value gap is equivalent to the relaxation time of the time-averaged transition semigroup. We show that, moreover, the inverse singular value gap of the two-point motion is equivalent to the relaxation time of the non-averaged transition semigroup, and that it provides a lower bound on the usual spectral gap of the generator. We then introduce a method for deriving lower bounds on singular value gaps for Markov processes with degenerate noise that is based on the concept of a first- and second-order collapse of the generator. It follows ideas from hypocoercivity developed in a previous series of works but is simpler and more broadly applicable. In contrast to previous results, it includes settings with non-vanishing first-order collapse, and thus applies directly to Markov chains (in continuous time), but also to diffusion processes and piecewise-deterministic Markov processes. Our approach yields sharp upper and lower bounds for several classes of examples. First applications include the proof of a conjecture by Diaconis and Miclo on a square-root speed-up for lifted random walks on abelian groups, as well as bounds on relaxation times of switching flows perturbed by noise and of non-reversible diffusion processes.

entry.title: Robust Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Label-Flip Attacks

link.title: Robust Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Label-Flip Attacks

entry.content:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. However, recent works have shown that DPO can be easily manipulated by adversarial preference label flip attacks, which are specifically designed to mislead the learner toward an attacker-chosen target policy. To address this issue, we design robust DPO methods that can defend against such attacks. Building on the property that lable flips induce parameter-independent gradient shifts in log-linear DPO, we propose Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which removes the $K$ highest-impact pairs, and Soft-Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which smoothly downweights them. We establish deterministic gradient perturbation bounds uniformly over all attack sets containing at most $K$ flips, explicitly separating defense-induced bias from surviving attack effects. Under bounded-region assumptions, these bounds yield time-uniform parameter and policy deviation guarantees. We further quantify how quadratic regularization improves curvature while introducing additional bias. Experiments on Stanford Human Preferences, HH-RLHF, and UltraFeedback-Binarized validate our analysis.

Read more

entry.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. However, recent works have shown that DPO can be easily manipulated by adversarial preference label flip attacks, which are specifically designed to mislead the learner toward an attacker-chosen target policy. To address this issue, we design robust DPO methods that can defend against such attacks. Building on the property that lable flips induce parameter-independent gradient shifts in log-linear DPO, we propose Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which removes the $K$ highest-impact pairs, and Soft-Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which smoothly downweights them. We establish deterministic gradient perturbation bounds uniformly over all attack sets containing at most $K$ flips, explicitly separating defense-induced bias from surviving attack effects. Under bounded-region assumptions, these bounds yield time-uniform parameter and policy deviation guarantees. We further quantify how quadratic regularization improves curvature while introducing additional bias. Experiments on Stanford Human Preferences, HH-RLHF, and UltraFeedback-Binarized validate our analysis.

entry.title: Robust Functional Ward’s Linkages with Applications in EEG data Clustering

link.title: Robust Functional Ward’s Linkages with Applications in EEG data Clustering

entry.content:
This paper proposes two robust linkage criteria, termed functional Ward-type linkages, for hierarchical clustering of grouped functional data, where each clustering unit is represented by a set of curves. Ordinary Ward\textquotesingle s linkage defines the cluster dissimilarity between two clusters as the increase in the sum of squared errors (SSE) upon merging, which can be interpreted graphically as an increase in within-cluster dispersion. Motivated by this principle, the proposed linkages measure the weighted increase in band width required to construct a common band containing the central representatives of two candidate clusters. To reduce the influence of outliers, the central curves are selected separately within each cluster by leveraging the magnitude-shape outlyingness measure and the modified band depth, respectively. Simulations and two EEG data analyses demonstrate the robustness and competitive performance of the proposed methods under a range of contamination settings.

Read more

entry.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation

link.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation

entry.content:
We introduce SNACK, a string representation for probabilistic graph generation that enables sequence models to generate and model graphs with discrete node and edge features. SNACK linearizes graphs by encoding the nonzero entries of the lower-triangular adjacency matrix, establishing a bijective correspondence between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices. This design enables invalid logit masking to enforce structural constraints–such as chemical valence and ordering rules–guaranteeing 100% valid generated sequences. SNACK also enables principled string-based GFlowNet training by explicitly accounting for node-ordering symmetries. Across standard graph-generation tasks and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks, SNACK achieves competitive sample quality, while substantially improving the throughput of GFlowNet training relative to graph-based generation. Probing analyses further show that models trained on SNACK encode meaningful local and global graph structure despite receiving only sequential supervision. These results position SNACK as a practical framework for probabilistic graph generation with deep sequence models.

Read more

entry.title: Scalable Bayesian Clustering for Integrative Analysis of Multi-View Data

link.title: Scalable Bayesian Clustering for Integrative Analysis of Multi-View Data

entry.content:
In the era of Big Data, scalable and accurate clustering algorithms for high-dimensional data are essential. We present new Bayesian Distance Clustering (BDC) models and inference algorithms with improved scalability while maintaining the predictive accuracy of modern Bayesian nonparametric models. Unlike traditional methods, BDC models the distance between observations rather than the observations directly, offering a compromise between the scalability of distance-based methods and the enhanced predictive power and probabilistic interpretation of model-based methods. However, existing BDC models still rely on performing inference on the partition model to group observations into clusters. The support of this partition model grows exponentially with the dataset’s size, complicating posterior space exploration and leading to many costly likelihood evaluations. Inspired by $k$-medoids, we propose using tessellations in discrete space to simplify inference by focusing the learning task on finding the best tessellation centers, or “medoids”. Additionally, we extend our models to effectively handle multi-view data, such as data comprised of clusters that evolve across time, enhancing their applicability to complex datasets. The real data application in numismatics demonstrates the efficacy of our approach.

Read more
